title: The fifty per cent wall: a reciprocal tariff and a Russian-oil tranche, built under two orders and one emergency about Ukraine
summary: Executive Order 14257 of 2 April 2025 imposed a duty on all imports from all trading partners of at least 10 per cent, with higher rates for dozens of countries. Executive Order 14329 of 6 August 2025 added a further 25 per cent ad valorem on articles of India alone, effective 21 days later — 27 August 2025 — on the finding that "the Government of India is currently directly or indirectly importing Russian Federation oil". The second order was made under the national emergency declared in EO 14066 about Russia's actions in Ukraine, not under any trade emergency, and India is the only country it names. Both were terminated on 20 February 2026.
claimAtLaunch: EO 14329 states its own objective in its own terms: the additional duty on India is "necessary and appropriate" to deal with the national emergency described in EO 14066 — the threat to United States national security and foreign policy posed by Russia's actions against Ukraine — and that imposing it "will more effectively deal with" that emergency.
whatHappened: The 25 per cent India tranche took effect 27 August 2025 and stacked on the reciprocal rate, reaching 50 per cent. It ran until Executive Order 14389 of 20 February 2026 provided that the additional ad valorem duties imposed under IEEPA in EO 14257 and EO 14329, among seven other orders, "shall no longer be in effect and, as soon as practicable, shall no longer be collected". The national emergencies themselves were expressly left standing; only the duties went.
assessmentNote: Scored no-objective from India's side, which is the side this instrument measures. EO 14329 has an objective and states it, but the objective is a change in Russian conduct toward Ukraine pursued through a duty on Indian goods, so nothing about India's condition is what it set out to move. There is no Indian measure here to have worked or failed. What the record holds is a shock and its dates.
caseFor: The instrument was aimed and it was withdrawn, and both facts belong in the record. The rate applied for under six months, not for a term, and the emergency it was made under is one India is not party to — so a reader treating 50 per cent as a settled condition of the external sector would be reading a peak as a level. The orders also did what tariff orders are supposed to do in a negotiation: a framework for an interim agreement followed on 6 February 2026, before the orders were terminated.
caseAgainst: For the period it ran this was the highest rate applied to any United States trading partner, and the mechanism is the part that does not wash out with the rate. The second tranche was not a finding about Indian trade practice: it names India's purchases from a third country, under an emergency declared about that third country, and no other purchaser of Russian crude was named. That makes the exposure political rather than commercial, and it is India-specific in a way no other shock in this instrument is — every other one is shared with the peer panel and can be netted against it. This one confounds every external-sector reading for FY2026 and FY2027 whatever rate finally settles.
shockExposure: India-specific in severity and in mechanism. Cannot be netted out by peer comparison and must be carried as a standalone confound for FY2026 and FY2027 external-sector assessments.

title: IEEPA does not authorise the President to impose tariffs, and every duty India faced under it ended the same day
summary: On 20 February 2026 the Supreme Court of the United States held, in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorise the President to impose tariffs. The Court reasoned that the taxing power is Congress's, that the Government conceded no inherent presidential tariff power in peacetime, and that in IEEPA's half century "no President has invoked the statute to impose any tariffs". Executive Order 14389 was issued the same day, ending the duties imposed under IEEPA in nine orders, including both that applied to India.
whatHappened: The judgment in the Court of International Trade line was affirmed. Chief Justice Roberts delivered the opinion of the Court on the constitutional framing and on the major-questions reasoning; the decision was against the Government. Justice Kavanaugh, dissenting, wrote that the decision "might not prevent Presidents from imposing most if not all of these same sorts of tariffs under other statutory authorities", and named section 122, section 201 and section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The first of those was used the same day: Proclamation 11012 of 20 February 2026 imposed a ten per cent surcharge under section 122, taking effect four days later on 24 February.
assessmentNote: A judgment of a foreign court is not an Indian measure and had no objective with respect to India at all — the petitioners were two American small businesses and five more with twelve States. Recorded because it is the event that removed the legal basis for the largest India-specific external shock in the instrument, and because a reader who has L-0184 without this one would carry a 50 per cent rate forward past the date it ceased to exist.
caseFor: The ruling is the reason the 50 per cent did not become a structural condition, and it is a durable one: it removes an authority rather than a rate, so the same instrument cannot simply be re-aimed. The reasoning is about the delegation, not about India, which means India's exposure to it does not depend on the state of the bilateral relationship.
caseAgainst: It removed one authority and the dissent named three replacements in the opinion itself, two of which were used within five months — section 122 four days later and section 301 in July. The rate India faces has since been set three separate times by three separate statutes, so what the ruling delivered was not relief but a change of instrument, and each successor has its own duration and its own exit. Reading this as the end of the tariff exposure would repeat the error of reading the 50 per cent as a level.

title: A ten per cent surcharge with a hundred-and-fifty-day fuse: section 122 used to its statutory maximum, and allowed to lapse
summary: Proclamation 11012 of 20 February 2026 imposed a ten per cent ad valorem surcharge on all articles imported into the United States under section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, effective 12:01 a.m. on 24 February 2026 and expiring 12:01 a.m. on 24 July 2026 "unless the effective period of such surcharge is extended by an Act of the Congress". Section 122 caps a surcharge at 15 per cent and its period at 150 days, and requires that it be applied consistently with the principle of nondiscriminatory treatment. The interval 24 February to 24 July 2026 is 150 days exactly. No Act extended it and it lapsed.
assessmentNote: A United States balance-of-payments measure, not an Indian one, and applied to all trading partners rather than to India. There is no Indian objective to score. It is in the ledger because for five months it was the rate Indian exporters actually paid, and because its expiry is the reason the rate changed again in July.
caseFor: This was the least India-specific tariff India faced in the whole episode, and that is a substantive difference rather than a technicality: section 122 requires nondiscriminatory application, so for 150 days Indian goods carried the same surcharge as everyone else's, at a rate below both the 50 per cent peak and the 18 per cent the February framework contemplated. The statute also did what a bounded delegation is meant to do — it ran to its limit and stopped without anyone having to stop it.
caseAgainst: The bound is on the instrument, not on the policy. Section 122's ceiling and fuse were reached and exhausted rather than restraining anything: the rate chosen was 10 of a permitted 15 per cent, the period taken was 150 of a permitted 150 days, and the day it expired a section 301 action took effect at the same moment. An exporter's exposure did not lapse; only the statute under it changed. The nondiscrimination requirement also cuts the other way — it means the surcharge was not a concession to India and was never available as one.
shockExposure: Applied to all trading partners, so unlike L-0184 this one IS shared with the peer panel and can be netted against it.
caveat: The 150-day figure is the statutory maximum and the proclamation took all of it; it is not an estimate. Counted from the effective date: 24 February to 24 March is 28 days, then 31, 30, 31 and 30 to 24 July — 150. The United States Court of International Trade struck down the section 122 tariffs in May 2026 and that decision was under appeal; this record does not rest on the litigation and no document from it has been retrieved here, so nothing about the appeal's outcome is stated.

title: India adopts a forced-labour import prohibition and is placed in the lower tier of the tariff that replaced the surcharge
summary: The United States Trade Representative determined action in section 301 investigations of 60 economies over the failure to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on importing goods made with forced labour. India was investigated among the 60 and was found, with 53 others, to have failed both limbs. It then adopted a forced-labour import prohibition after the 5 June 2026 proposed action was published, and on that basis was placed in the ten per cent tier rather than the 12.5 per cent tier. The duties took effect at 12:01 a.m. eastern time on 24 July 2026 — the moment the section 122 surcharge expired.
claimAtLaunch: The determination states the criterion for the lower tier in its own terms: an economy that "imposes a forced labor import prohibition, has committed to impose and enforce such a prohibition through an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART), or has imposed a partial regime with the effect of preventing the importation of certain forced labor goods" receives 10 per cent rather than 12.5 per cent. India's entry reads that the determination was made "including India's adoption of a forced labor import prohibition subsequent to the publication of the June 5, 2026 FRN".
whatHappened: Sixteen other economies join India in the ten per cent tier. The action carries no statutory expiry, unlike the section 122 surcharge it displaced, and exempts articles already subject to section 232 duties along with a list of raw materials and, after comment, chemical products in their pharmaceutical applications only.
assessmentNote: Two measures meet here and neither is scorable as an Indian objective. The section 301 action is a United States measure with a United States objective. India's adoption of the prohibition is an Indian measure, but the record cannot establish what it was adopted FOR: no Indian announcement of it has been retrieved in this run, and the only document that describes it is the American determination that rewarded it. Scoring an Indian measure on a foreign agency's account of it would be inferring an objective, which is the thing the value exists to refuse.
caseFor: Whatever it was adopted for, the prohibition is the reason India pays 10 rather than 12.5 per cent, and it is a rule against importing goods made with forced labour — a thing worth having on its own terms and one India had not previously had. The mechanism is also more durable than what it replaced: a section 301 action rests on a finding about conduct, so conduct can end it, where the section 122 surcharge could only be waited out.
caseAgainst: The instrument that produced the prohibition was a tariff threat from a third country, and the finding against India on both limbs stands unchanged — the tier moved, the determination that India had failed to impose and enforce did not. A prohibition adopted between a proposed action and a final one, and evidenced here only by the foreign determination citing it, is a commitment whose enforcement nobody has yet measured. And the replacement carries no sunset: India exchanged a duty that was going to expire in any case for one that will not.

title: The 6 February framework: an eighteen per cent rate promised under an order struck down fourteen days later, and an interim agreement not concluded since
summary: On 6 February 2026 the United States and India announced a framework for an Interim Agreement. Its central rate term is specific about its instrument: the United States "will apply a reciprocal tariff rate of 18 percent under Executive Order 14257 of April 2, 2025 ... as amended, on originating goods of India". Removal of the reciprocal tariff on generic pharmaceuticals, gems and diamonds and aircraft parts was made subject to "the successful conclusion of the Interim Agreement". EO 14257's duties were terminated on 20 February 2026, fourteen days later.
claimAtLaunch: That the framework would be promptly implemented and the Interim Agreement finalised, en route to a broader Bilateral Trade Agreement launched on 13 February 2025. India's side of the framework is tariff elimination or reduction on all United States industrial goods and a listed range of food and agricultural products, action on named non-tariff barriers, and an intent to "purchase $500 billion of U.S. energy products, aircraft and aircraft parts, precious metals, technology products, and coking coal over the next 5 years".
whatHappened: Three commitment states, kept separate because they resolve differently. (a) NOT YET DUE: the $500 billion purchase intent runs five years from February 2026, so its trigger is February 2031 and nothing about it is testable now. The determination on standards acceptability is due within six months of entry into force, which has not begun to run. (b) DUE AND UNDELIVERED: the Interim Agreement itself. Both sides targeted July 2026 and the section 122 surcharge's 24 July expiry was the working deadline; USTR's own 2026 press-release index, retrieved 4 August 2026, records no announcement of a concluded agreement with India, while recording concluded or early-harvest agreements with other partners in the same window. (c) The 18 per cent rate is neither: it was applied, and then its authority was extinguished by a court ruling about a different case. India's rate has since been set by section 122 and then by section 301, at 10 per cent under each.
assessmentNote: Too-early rather than failed, and the distinction is the obstacle. What is missing is a concluded Interim Agreement, and the evidence that would settle whether the framework produced one is evidence time accumulates — further negotiating rounds, or their absence past a point where absence means something. Not awaiting-adjudication: nothing is pending before any body outside the two governments. Not failed: the framework's own headline term is a rate India is currently beating, so a reader told this failed would draw the wrong inference about the direction of the outcome. What can be said now is that the deliverable is late and the instrument it named no longer exists.
caseFor: The framework was announced at 50 per cent and India now pays 10, and every step of that path runs through a negotiation this framework opened. The pharmaceutical, gems and aircraft-parts carve-outs are still live commitments rather than lapsed ones, and the BTA track it reaffirms has been running since February 2025. A framework is by construction a statement of intent, and holding it to a delivery date it did not set would be scoring it against an objective it did not claim.
caseAgainst: The central term was drafted against a specific instrument by number, and that instrument was void within a fortnight — which means the promise as written could not be performed, and nothing retrieved shows it renegotiated onto a surviving authority. The valuable terms are all conditional on a conclusion that has not happened: pharmaceuticals, gems and aircraft parts turn on "successful conclusion", and the generic-pharmaceutical outcome is additionally contingent on the findings of a section 232 investigation that is a United States process India does not control. Against that, India's own side of the framework — tariff elimination on all US industrial goods, named non-tariff barriers, a $500 billion purchase intent — is written without conditions.
differentFactsNote: Both readings accept the text, the dates and the termination. The disagreement is whether a framework whose named instrument was struck down is a live commitment or a dead letter, and that is a judgement about what a framework is, not a dispute about what happened.

title: India was tariffed for buying Russian crude, and India does not publish how much Russian crude it buys
summary: The additional 25 per cent duty of EO 14329 rested on a finding of fact about India — that it "is currently directly or indirectly importing Russian Federation oil" — and the duty was calibrated to that finding rather than to any quantity of it. India's own petroleum statistics do not carry the quantity. The Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell's monthly Snapshot of India's Oil & Gas data for June 2026, retrieved 4 August 2026, publishes crude imports in volume and value and by refinery, and contains no country-of-origin breakdown and no occurrence of the word Russia.
assessmentNote: Not a measure. This is an episode in the sense the type admits: a foreign finding of fact about India, and the state of Indian publication against it. Nothing here was announced to achieve anything, so there is no objective to test.
caseFor: The absence is a reporting-format fact rather than a suppression: PPAC's monthly snapshot has never been an origin-of-imports publication, and origin data for crude is commercially sensitive and genuinely held by refiners rather than by the ministry. India is not unusual in this — few states publish monthly crude imports by counterparty — and the quantity is estimated publicly by commercial trackers whose figures are widely reported.
caseAgainst: A duty was levied on the entire Indian export basket on the strength of a quantity that the Indian state does not publish and the American order did not state. Neither government put a number on the record, so the proportionality of the measure to the conduct it was aimed at cannot be tested from official sources at all, and the only figures available are commercial estimates that are not official on either side. For an instrument that ties every rendered number to a source and a tier, that is the finding: the single largest India-specific external shock in the corpus rests on a fact with no official measurement behind it.

title: The India-China merchandise deficit has two values, and the gap between them is larger than most bilateral relationships
summary: For calendar 2024 India's own submitted figures give a bilateral merchandise deficit with China of US$112.064bn. China's own submitted figures give a bilateral surplus with India of US$102.464bn. The two balances differ by US$9.600bn, up from US$6.584bn in 2023. Part is the ordinary CIF-against-FOB valuation convention, which is visible operating in both directions. The remainder is not: on the India-to-China flow China records 20.80 per cent more arriving than India records leaving, against 5.40 per cent on the flow the other way.
assessmentNote: No measure and no objective — this is a state of the measurement, not a policy that was announced to do something. It is a ledger record rather than only a provenance record because the quantity it concerns is cited constantly in argument about the relationship, and a reader reaching for 'the' deficit needs to meet the fact that there are two before they meet either.
caseFor: The divergence is ordinary in kind and mostly ordinary in size. Bilateral statistics diverge between every pair of countries for reasons that are documented and uncontroversial: the importer values CIF and the exporter FOB, so the importer's figure is systematically higher, and that is exactly the pattern here in both directions. The larger residual has a well-known and plausible mechanism in entrepot trade through Hong Kong, whose scale — India's reported exports to Hong Kong were US$6.498bn in 2024 — is comfortably sufficient to contain it. Nothing here suggests either statistical authority is misreporting.
caseAgainst: Ordinary in kind is not the same as immaterial in size, and the size is the point. A US$9.600bn discrepancy is larger than India's entire reported merchandise trade with most of its partners, and it sits inside the single number that carries the most weight in argument about this relationship. The 20.80 per cent excess on Indian exports is not explained by valuation and the entrepot account remains a sized candidate rather than a demonstrated cause, because neither side publishes the origin-basis data that would settle it. And the direction matters politically: the deficit that India cites is the larger of the two available figures, and the surplus China cites is the smaller — each government's own statistics flatter its own account of the imbalance.
differentFactsNote: This is the genuine article and not a difference of emphasis. The two sides publish different numbers for the same flow in the same year on the same commodity basis, and each is authoritative for its own jurisdiction. The instrument carries both, computes the gap because the gap's size is evidence about its cause, and picks neither.

title: Calendar 2025 has an Indian figure and no Chinese one, so it is not a mirror and must not be read as one
summary: India reports importing US$149.495bn from China in calendar 2025 and exporting US$18.086bn to it — an Indian-basis deficit of US$131.409bn, and a 17.75 per cent rise in imports over 2024. China had filed no calendar-2025 annual return with UN Comtrade as at 4 August 2026. The 2025 figure is therefore single-sided: there is nothing to disagree with it, which is not the same as agreement.
assessmentNote: A state of the measurement, not a measure. Recorded separately from L-0190 rather than folded into it precisely because folding it in is the error: a table showing 2023, 2024 and 2025 with two columns for the first two years and one for the third invites the reader to treat the 2025 column as the settled figure, when it is the only figure.
caseFor: The Indian series is not weakened by the absence of a Chinese one. It is India's own submission on the same basis it has used in every prior year, it is internally consistent with 2023 and 2024, and a 17.75 per cent rise is large but not anomalous against a 4.10 per cent rise the year before. Waiting for a counterparty's return before reading one's own statistics would make every recent year unusable.
caseAgainst: Every previously testable year has been wrong by billions, in a consistent direction, and the untested year is being read as though that record did not exist. On 2024's evidence the Chinese-basis import figure would be roughly five per cent lower and the Chinese-basis balance roughly nine per cent narrower than the Indian one — so the single-sided 2025 deficit of US$131.409bn is, on the pattern, an upper bound presented without the qualification the two earlier years both carry. The rise itself is the figure most likely to be quoted and the least likely to be quoted with the caveat.
differentFactsNote: There is no second account to differ with. That is the record's subject rather than a reason to mark it: an absent counterparty figure is an absence, not a dispute, and marking it differentFacts would put a single-sided number in the same category as the genuine mirror in L-0190 — which is the exact confusion this record exists to prevent.

title: India runs a merchandise surplus with every immediate neighbour except Myanmar
summary: On India's own reported figures for calendar 2024, India exported US$25.592bn to the six immediate neighbours other than Pakistan and imported US$5.745bn from them — a surplus of US$19.847bn, and exports 4.5 times imports. Five of the six are surpluses: Bangladesh +9.456, Nepal +6.084, Sri Lanka +3.747, Bhutan +0.738, Maldives +0.733. Myanmar is the single exception at -0.911, and is the only neighbour in this set from which India buys more than it sells.
assessmentNote: A measured position, not a measure. No Indian policy was announced with the objective of producing a regional trade surplus, so there is nothing here to have worked or failed. The record exists because 'Neighbourhood First' is a stated doctrine and its trade dimension is routinely described without a figure attached, and because the Myanmar exception is invisible in any regional aggregate.
caseFor: A surplus of this shape is what the size asymmetry predicts and is not in itself a policy outcome. India's economy is roughly an order of magnitude larger than the next-largest in the set, the neighbours are land-linked to it, and Nepal and Bhutan in particular trade with the world substantially through India. Read as delivery, the numbers are also real: US$25.592bn of Indian goods reaching neighbouring markets is the material content of a neighbourhood policy, and it is concentrated in the two largest partners rather than spread thin.
caseAgainst: A surplus of 4.5 to 1 is the arithmetic of a market, not of an integration. The doctrine is stated as mutual benefit and the flow it produces is overwhelmingly one-directional, which is the standing complaint of every partner in the set and the reason each has pursued alternatives. The single deficit is with Myanmar, where the trade is dominated by primary commodities rather than by any market India opened. And the aggregate is the least informative way to read it: five surpluses and one deficit summed into one figure conceals that the exception exists at all.
caveat: The component figures are US$ billion rounded to three decimals and the totals are computed on the unrounded submissions, so summing the printed components gives 25.591 and 5.746 against printed totals of 25.592 and 5.745, and a balance of 19.845 against 19.847. The totals are the ones computed from source and are correct; the reconstruction is what is lossy. Stated so a reader adding the column finds an explanation rather than a discrepancy — the basis is set out in P-120, which this record cites.

title: Half the neighbourhood does not report its trade, and every neighbour that does records less arriving than India records sending
summary: Of the six immediate neighbours other than Pakistan, three had filed calendar-2024 annual returns with UN Comtrade as at 4 August 2026 and three had not. Bangladesh's last annual return naming India is 2018; Nepal's is 2022; Bhutan's is 2023. For the three that do report — Sri Lanka, Maldives and Myanmar — each records receiving substantially LESS from India than India records sending: 3.738 against 4.715, 0.502 against 0.825, and 0.359 against 0.609. That is the opposite direction from the India-China mirror, where the importer's figure is the higher one as the valuation convention predicts.
assessmentNote: A state of the measurement across an arc, not a measure. Recorded separately from L-0192 because it is a different claim about the same figures: L-0192 says what the position is, this says how much of it can be checked. Half of it cannot be checked at all, and where it can, it does not agree.
caseFor: Neither half of this is evidence of anything wrong with India's statistics. Non-reporting to Comtrade is a statistical-capacity and submission-schedule question for the partner, not a statement about the trade, and small economies file late or not at all across the whole system. On the divergence, the three partners are among the smallest reporters in the set, and a partner that under-records imports is describing its own customs coverage rather than contradicting India's export records. India's figures are internally consistent across all six partners and across years.
caseAgainst: The direction is the problem, and it is consistent across all three testable partners. The valuation convention predicts the importer's figure is HIGHER, because it includes freight and insurance; here it is lower every time, by 26, 64 and 69 per cent of the partner's own figure. Whatever explains that, it is not freight, and it is not a rounding question at these magnitudes. Nothing in the record establishes a cause and none is asserted — but a regional trade position of which half is unverifiable and the verifiable half disagrees in a single direction is a weaker evidentiary base than a single figure suggests. The three non-reporters include the two largest partners in the set by value.
differentFactsNote: Genuine and partial. For Sri Lanka, Maldives and Myanmar two governments publish figures for the same flow in the same year on the same commodity basis and they disagree; the instrument carries both and picks neither. For Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan there is no second account to disagree with, which is an absence rather than a dispute — the two states are kept apart here for the same reason L-0190 and L-0191 are kept apart.

unmeasured.why: None had filed a calendar-2024 annual return with UN Comtrade as at 4 August 2026, and each zero was localised before it was recorded rather than assumed. Relaxing the partner from India to the world left all three at zero, so none is an India-specific omission. Relaxing the period is what flips each, and it flips at a different year for each: Bhutan reports 2023, Nepal reports 2022, and Bangladesh's last return naming India is 2018 — confirmed by walking back year by year until the query went non-zero at US$9.409bn, which also serves as the positive control that the reporter code and query shape are right.

title: TEPA carries the first investment commitment in an Indian trade agreement: US$100bn over fifteen years, and the first tranche is not due until 2035
summary: The India-EFTA Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement entered into force on 1 October 2025, two years after signature. It carries an investment objective of US$100bn into India over fifteen years and the facilitation of one million direct jobs, which the Ministry of Commerce describes as making it "the first trade agreement to incorporate a firm investment commitment". The four EFTA states — Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland — have a combined population smaller than Mumbai's, a point the Minister made himself at the entry-into-force summit.
claimAtLaunch: US$100bn of investment mobilised into India over fifteen years from entry into force, and one million direct jobs facilitated, monitored through an investment facilitation mechanism. The Minister's stated ground for calling it pioneering is that it is "the first trade agreement to incorporate a firm investment commitment, thereby balancing interests and ensuring fairness between partners".
whatHappened: COMMITMENT STATE (a) — NOT YET DUE, AND THE TRIGGER IS NAMED. The agreement entered into force on 1 October 2025 and the fifteen-year horizon runs to 1 October 2040. Nothing about the target is testable at ten months, and this record does not attempt to test it. What can be recorded now is the structure and the clock. On the second anniversary of signature, 10 March 2026, the Ministry restated the target unchanged and reported implementation as proceeding; it published no cumulative figure against it, which at that point is the expected state rather than a finding.
assessmentNote: Too-early in its strict sense: the measure is in force and the obstacle is elapsed time and the evidence time accumulates. Not awaiting-adjudication — nothing is pending before any body outside the parties. The record exists NOW rather than in 2040 because a commitment with a fifteen-year horizon is precisely the kind that is announced once and never revisited, and the point of entering it early is to fix what was promised, by when, and how it is to be measured, before any of those become matters of recollection.
caseFor: An investment target written into a trade agreement is a genuine novelty in Indian practice and it is the answer to the standing objection that FTAs deliver market access outward and nothing inward. It is sized, dated and given a monitoring mechanism rather than left as an aspiration, and the counterparties are four high-income economies whose outward FDI is real money rather than a projection. Ten months is not a basis for scepticism about a fifteen-year commitment.
caseAgainst: The words the two sides use for it are not the same word. The Ministry calls it a "firm investment commitment"; the joint framing is an "objective" and an aim to "mobilise", which is an undertaking to try. Nothing retrieved here establishes a consequence for missing it, and an obligation with no remedy is a target. The horizon is also long enough to outlast the governments that signed it and every official who negotiated it, and the first checkpoint is a decade out — so the practical position is that nothing about this is falsifiable for ten years, which is a property of the commitment rather than a criticism of the parties.

unmeasured.what: Cumulative EFTA-origin FDI into India since 1 October 2025, measured on the basis the agreement's investment facilitation mechanism uses
unmeasured.why: No figure against the target has been published by either side, and at ten months from entry into force none is due. The measurement basis itself is not established by anything retrieved here — whether the target counts gross inflows, net inflows, or announced intentions is the difference between a testable commitment and an untestable one, and the documents retrieved state the number without stating the basis.
unmeasured.wouldFill: The first report of the investment facilitation mechanism established under TEPA, or an RBI FDI series broken down to the four EFTA states on a stated basis.

Whichever comes first. If 2035 passes with no published cumulative figure, the commitment state moves from (a) to (b) and the absence of a measurement basis becomes the finding rather than a caveat.

title: "Merchandise trade with both Australia and the UAE has doubled since the signing" — true on a baseline two years before either signature, false on both years nearest it
summary: On the second anniversary of TEPA's signature the Prime Minister said: "Merchandise trade with both Australia and the UAE has doubled since the signing of FTAs with these countries." India's own figures as submitted to UN Comtrade support that on one baseline and contradict it on the two nearest the signings. The UAE CEPA was signed on 18 February 2022 and the Australia ECTA on 2 April 2022. Two-way merchandise trade in calendar 2025 stood at 2.26 times its CY2020 level for the UAE and 2.21 times for Australia — but only 1.38 and 1.08 times CY2021, the last full year before either signature, and 1.11 and 0.85 times CY2022, the year of signature. Australian two-way trade in 2025 is below where it was when ECTA was signed.
assessmentNote: Contested rather than failed, and the reason is that the claim does not state its baseline. On a CY2020 base it is exactly right for both countries. On CY2021 and CY2022 it is wrong for both. The record does not choose, because choosing would require asserting a baseline the speaker did not give — and the honest finding is that a claim of this shape is unfalsifiable until the base year is named, which is itself the thing worth recording.
caseFor: A doubling from CY2020 is arithmetically correct on India's own submissions and CY2020 is not an absurd base: the agreements were negotiated through 2020 and 2021, and a speaker describing what a trade relationship looks like now against what it looked like when the process began is making an ordinary comparison. Neither agreement was signed in a vacuum in 2022 — the UAE CEPA negotiation opened in September 2021 — so "since the signing" as a loose marker for the whole arc is a reading the words will bear. The UAE growth is also substantial on any base: 68.5 to 94.5 billion dollars in four years is not a rounding of the truth.
caseAgainst: CY2020 is the deepest contraction in modern trade history and using it as a base makes almost any recovery look like a doubling. It also precedes both signatures by two years, so "since the signing" points at it only by straining. On the two baselines the words actually indicate the claim fails, and for Australia it fails badly: 1.08 times CY2021 is not a doubling but noise, and 0.85 times CY2022 means two-way trade with Australia has FALLEN since ECTA was signed. Presenting a COVID-trough comparison as the effect of an agreement signed two years later attributes to the agreement a recovery that would have happened without it.
differentFactsNote: There is no dispute about any figure here. Both readings use the same series, India's own, and disagree only about which year "since the signing" points at. That is a difference about the meaning of a phrase, not about the world, which is why this is not a differentFacts pair even though it looks like one at a distance.
caveat: The test uses calendar years because UN Comtrade's annual series is calendar-based on both sides, and Indian trade statistics are conventionally reported on an April-March financial year. A financial-year test would move each figure and could move a ratio near the boundary; none of the ratios here is near the boundary — the closest to 2.00 on a signature-adjacent base is 1.38 — so the conclusion does not turn on the calendar convention. It is stated because the reader should not have to assume it.

title: Defence exports reach ₹38,424 crore against a ₹50,000 crore target for 2029, and the private sector's share falls nineteen points in the year it is reported as rising
summary: Defence exports in FY2025-26 were ₹38,424 crore, up ₹14,802 crore or 62.66 per cent on FY2024-25's ₹23,622 crore, exported to more than 80 countries by 145 firms. Defence public sector undertakings contributed ₹21,071 crore and the private sector ₹17,353 crore. The Ministry reports the private sector's contribution as "up by 14 per cent", which is true of its value: it rose from ₹15,233 crore, a gain of 13.92 per cent. Its SHARE of the total fell from 64.49 per cent to 45.16 per cent in the same year, because DPSU exports rose 151 per cent from ₹8,389 crore.
claimAtLaunch: A target of ₹50,000 crore in defence exports by 2029, restated by the Ministry in June 2026 as current.
whatHappened: COMMITMENT STATE (a) — NOT YET DUE, TRIGGER NAMED: 2029. At FY2025-26 the running total is 76.8 per cent of the target with three financial years to run, which requires compound growth of 9.17 per cent a year to FY2028-29 against 62.66 per cent delivered in the year just reported. On the trajectory reported, the target is not the binding constraint.
assessmentNote: Too-early on the target, which is the record's scored object: the measure is in force, the obstacle is elapsed time, and three years of export figures are exactly the evidence time accumulates. Not partly — a target with three years left is not partially achieved, it is unresolved. The composition finding below is not scored, because no objective was ever stated for the DPSU-private split.
caseFor: The figures are internally consistent and the release does not overstate them. Every derived number in it was recomputed here and every one is right: the components sum to the totals in both years, 62.66 per cent is the exact year-on-year rise, the two shares are exact and sum to 100, and the 151 per cent and 13.3 per cent growth figures are correct. That is worth saying in an instrument that exists partly to catch the opposite. On substance, ₹38,424 crore against ₹686 crore a decade earlier is a real change in a sector that had almost no export base, the exporter count rose from 128 firms to 145, and reaching 76.8 per cent of a 2029 target in FY2025-26 is ahead of a straight line.
caseAgainst: The composition moved in the direction the policy exists to move away from. Aatmanirbharta is argued as building a private defence industrial base, and in the year of the record total the private sector's share of exports fell 19.33 percentage points — from roughly two-thirds to under half — because state-owned undertakings grew 151 per cent against the private sector's 13.92. The release reports the private figure as "up by 14 per cent" and does not report the share at all, which is accurate and is the less informative of the two available framings. And the headline is a single year: a 62.66 per cent rise concentrated in DPSUs may be one or two large contracts rather than a trend, and nothing in the release distinguishes those.

unmeasured.what: What the ₹50,000 crore target counts — order value, delivered value, or export authorisations issued
unmeasured.why: Neither the release announcing the FY2025-26 figure nor the June 2026 restatement of the target states the measurement basis, and the two are cited together as though commensurable. An export figure built on authorisations and a target built on realised value are different quantities, and the difference decides whether the target is close or already met.
unmeasured.wouldFill: The Defence Production and Export Promotion Policy or the Department of Defence Production's own definition of the export series, stating what is counted and at what point in a contract.

unmeasured.what: Which countries the exports go to, and in what value
unmeasured.why: The release states exports reached "more than 80 countries" and gives no distribution. A count of destinations does not distinguish a broad export base from a small number of large buyers plus a long tail of minor sales.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A country-wise breakdown from the Department of Defence Production, or India's own arms-export reporting to the UN Register of Conventional Arms.

title: India's defence exports are measured by three instruments that measure three different things, and SIPRI says in terms that its own must not be compared with the others
summary: The Ministry of Defence publishes defence exports as a rupee value: ₹38,424 crore for FY2025-26. SIPRI publishes Indian arms exports as a trend-indicator value, which its own sources-and-methods page states is "intended to represent the transfer of military resources rather than the financial value of the transfer" and which "should therefore not be directly compared with gross domestic product (GDP), military expenditure, sales values or the financial value of export licences". UN Comtrade carries a third figure on a currency basis — India's exports under HS chapter 93, arms and ammunition, were US$0.817bn in calendar 2025 — but chapter 93 is a commodity class, not a policy category, and excludes the aircraft, electronics and subsystems that make up much of what the Ministry counts.
assessmentNote: A state of the measurement, not a measure. No objective was announced about how defence exports are counted, so there is nothing here to have worked or failed. The record exists because the MoD figure and the SIPRI figure are placed side by side constantly in commentary about whether India is becoming an arms exporter, and that comparison is one SIPRI itself rules out.
caseFor: Three instruments for three purposes is not a defect. A finance ministry needs a currency value, a peace research institute tracking the flow of military capability needs a unit that does not move with prices or exchange rates, and a customs authority needs a commodity classification that works for every good. Each is fit for its own purpose and each publishes its method. SIPRI in particular is unusually explicit — the warning against comparison is on its own methods page, not buried — so a reader who checks the source is told not to do the thing.
caseAgainst: The comparison is made anyway, routinely, and the instrument that most often gets used as the check on the government's number is the one that cannot serve as one. A TIV is built from unit production costs of a reference set, discounts a second-hand weapon to 40 per cent of a new one, and is deliberately held constant over time so that trends stay comparable — none of which is a claim about money received. Reading a divergence between it and the rupee series as evidence that the rupee series is inflated is a category error, and reading agreement between them as corroboration is the same error with a friendlier conclusion. The customs figure is a genuine currency value and covers a different scope, so it cannot settle it either.
differentFactsNote: NOT a differentFacts pair, and the distinction is the point of the record. A differentFacts pair is two instruments measuring the SAME quantity and disagreeing — India and China on one trade flow, in P-119. This is two instruments measuring DIFFERENT quantities, where the divergence carries no information about either. Marking it differentFacts would file a category error as a dispute and invite exactly the averaging or picking that this record exists to refuse. It is equally not the single-sided case of L-0191: nothing here is unmeasured, and three parties publish.
caveat: This record deliberately does not place a SIPRI TIV figure beside the Ministry's rupee figure, and does not convert between the rupee, the dollar and the TIV. Doing either would perform the comparison the record is about. The HS 93 figure is given in its own currency and period — US$0.817bn, calendar 2025, against the Ministry's ₹38,424 crore for FY2025-26 — with no arithmetic relating them, because they differ in period, currency and scope at once and no single conversion addresses all three.

unmeasured.what: A currency-basis figure for Indian defence exports on the same scope the Ministry counts, published by anyone other than the Ministry
unmeasured.why: The only independent currency-basis series that reaches these goods is customs data, and customs classifies by commodity rather than by end use: HS chapter 93 captures arms and ammunition and leaves out the aircraft, avionics, radar and subsystems that make up much of the Ministry's total. There is therefore no second party publishing the same quantity, which is why this is not a mirror and cannot be made into one by choosing a better source.
unmeasured.wouldFill: An importing state's own record of what it paid India, or India's reporting to the UN Register of Conventional Arms with values attached. Either would be a genuine currency-basis counterpart and would make a differentFacts pair possible for the first time.

title: Three quantities are called indigenisation: one has a defined formula, one is a production total, and the headline share has no stated basis at all
summary: Defence Acquisition Procedure 2020 raised the minimum indigenous content required in each acquisition category and — this is the part usually left out — fixed how it is measured: "IC will now be calculated on 'Base Contract Price' i.e. Total Contract Price less taxes & duties". The minimums are Buy (Indian-IDDM) 50 per cent, up from 40; Buy (Indian) 50 per cent where the design is indigenous and 60 otherwise, up from 40; Buy & Make (Indian) 50 per cent of the Make portion; Buy (Global – Manufacture in India) 50 per cent of Buy plus Make; Buy (Global) 30 per cent for Indian vendors. Separately, the Ministry reports indigenous defence production rising from ₹46,429 crore in FY2014-15 to ₹1.78 lakh crore in FY2025-26, and states that "nearly 65% of defence equipment is now produced domestically, compared to import dependence of 65–70% earlier".
claimAtLaunch: That raising the indigenous-content minimums across categories, with a verification process and a stated calculation basis, would shift procurement toward domestic design and manufacture.
whatHappened: The basis for the CONTRACTUAL measure is defined and published, and this record says so plainly because a defined basis is worth recording as clearly as a missing one. The two figures usually quoted alongside it are different quantities. Indigenous production is a value aggregate, not a contractual share, and nothing in it is computed on Base Contract Price. The "nearly 65 per cent" is a share of "defence equipment", and no basis is stated for it anywhere retrieved here: not whether it is by value or by count, not whether the population is annual procurement or the standing inventory, and not what date "earlier" refers to in the 65-70 per cent it is compared against.
assessmentNote: Partly, and the split is between the two halves of the same reform. The measurement half worked: DAP 2020 set category minimums and fixed the calculation basis, and both are published and checkable. The reporting half did not follow: the figures the Ministry leads with are a production total and an unattributed equipment share, neither computed on the basis DAP defines, so the reform's own metric is not the one the public sees. Scored against the objective stated at announcement — a shift toward domestic design and manufacture, measured by indigenous content — which is testable in principle precisely because DAP defined it.
caseFor: The government did the hard part and did it explicitly. An indigenous-content rule is worthless without a formula, because every vendor would compute it differently and no bid would be comparable; DAP 2020 states the denominator, excludes taxes and duties so tax changes cannot move the number, and instituted a verification process. The category minimums rose by ten points across the board on a published table with the old and new figures side by side, which is an auditable commitment rather than a slogan. And the direction is not in doubt: production up from ₹46,429 crore to roughly 3.8 times that in eleven years is a real change in domestic output whatever share it represents.
caseAgainst: The number that governs procurement and the number that is published are not the same number, and only the second is ever quoted. "Nearly 65 per cent of defence equipment produced domestically" is the sentence that circulates, and it has no stated denominator, no stated population and no date for the baseline it improves on — so it cannot be checked, cannot be reproduced, and cannot be compared with the DAP figure it is taken to vindicate. A production total rising is consistent with the indigenous share falling if procurement rose faster, and nothing published lets a reader rule that out. The reform defined a metric and then reported against a different one.
differentFactsNote: Not a dispute: one government publishes all three figures and no one contradicts them. The relation between them is the incommensurability case — a per-contract contractual floor, a production aggregate and an equipment share are three different quantities, and the record's point is that they are read as one. NOTHING HERE IS PLACED SIDE BY SIDE AS CORROBORATION: that the production total rose while the DAP minimums rose is not evidence that the minimums are being met, and treating it as such is the same category error as reading a divergence between them as evidence of failure.

unmeasured.what: The basis of the "nearly 65 per cent of defence equipment produced domestically" figure
unmeasured.why: No denominator, population or baseline date is stated for it in anything retrieved here. By value or by count, of annual procurement or of standing inventory, and against what year — each choice gives a different number, and the figure is quoted as though it were one quantity.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A Ministry of Defence or Department of Defence Production statement of the series definition, or a Parliamentary answer giving the numerator and denominator.

unmeasured.why: DAP defines how IC is computed per contract and instituted verification, but no aggregate of verified IC across signed contracts is published. Without it, the minimums are known to be contractual conditions and not known to be outcomes.
unmeasured.wouldFill: An aggregate of verified indigenous content by acquisition category from the Department of Defence Production, or a CAG audit of IC verification.

caveat: "1.78 lakh crore" is stated to three significant figures while ₹46,429 crore is exact, so their ratio is determined only to about 3.82-3.84 and is written here as "roughly 3.8 times" rather than to more places than the source supports.

title: India has not been sanctioned under CAATSA for the S-400, and that is not the same as having been waived — the statute distinguishes three states and the public record separates only one
summary: Section 231(a) of the Countering America's Adversaries Through Sanctions Act provides that the President "shall impose five or more of the sanctions described in section 235" on a person determined to have knowingly engaged in a significant transaction with the Russian defence or intelligence sectors. India contracted for the S-400 in 2018. No sanction has been imposed. The statute makes three different things capable of producing that outcome, each with its own instrument: no determination under (a); a waiver under (b); or a delay under (c). Only the first would necessarily be visible from outside.
whatHappened: The three states, as the statute defines them. (a) NO DETERMINATION: the duty to sanction arises only once the President determines a significant transaction occurred, and nothing compels that determination to be made or announced. (b) WAIVER — and its conditions are the striking part: a waiver requires the President to submit to congressional committees both a written determination that it is in the vital national security interests of the United States or will further enforcement, AND "a certification that the Government of the Russian Federation has made significant efforts to reduce the number and intensity of cyber intrusions conducted by that Government". That second condition is a finding about RUSSIA, not about India, so a waiver for India turns on a judgement India cannot influence. (c) DELAY: available if the President certifies to the committees, not less frequently than every 180 days, that the person is substantially reducing its significant transactions.
assessmentNote: Not an Indian measure and not scorable as one — CAATSA is a United States statute with a United States objective. Recorded because the sentence "India got a CAATSA waiver" is common and, on everything retrieved here, unsupported: no waiver instrument has been located, and the absence of sanctions is not one.
caseFor: Nothing has happened to India under this statute in eight years, through two administrations and after the S-400 deliveries began, and at some point a consistent non-event is evidence about intent even without an instrument. The strategic reasoning is not hidden either: sanctioning India would be an unusual way to pursue an Indo-Pacific partnership. A reader who wants to know whether India faces CAATSA exposure in practice has a reasonable answer, which is that it has not materialised.
caseAgainst: An unexercised discretion is not a waiver and does not have a waiver's properties. A waiver under (b) is an instrument with a date, conditions and a submission to Congress; no determination under (a) is simply a decision not yet taken, and it can be taken later on the same facts, because the transaction does not expire. Collapsing the two turns a standing exposure into a settled question. The statutory language is mandatory once the determination is made — "shall impose five or more" — so the whole of India's protection lies in a determination not being made, which nothing published constrains.
differentFactsNote: No competing accounts of any fact. The disagreement in commentary is about what the absence of a sanction MEANS, and both readings accept that no sanction has been imposed and that no waiver instrument is public.

unmeasured.what: Whether a section 231(b) waiver or a section 231(c) delay has been issued in respect of India
unmeasured.why: Both are submissions to congressional committees rather than public actions, so their absence from the public record does not establish that they were not made. The absence CAN be established for the sanctions action itself: a determination under (a) followed by sanctions produces a published Federal Register notice, as the Department of State's notice of 7 April 2021 shows for Turkey's Presidency of Defense Industries, and a search of the Federal Register for CAATSA documents naming India returns nothing of that kind. The positive control is that same Turkey notice — the mechanism does produce a published instrument when it is used, so its absence for India is informative about sanctions and silent about waivers.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A congressional committee record of a submission under section 231(b) or (c) naming India, or a Presidential determination published under Executive Order 13849.

title: Emergency procurement: a ₹300 crore delegation with a stated clock, and two Ministry of Defence figures for the same thirteen contracts
summary: At a special meeting on 15 July 2020, convened over "the security environment due to prevailing situation along the Northern Borders", the Defence Acquisition Council delegated to the Armed Forces the power to progress urgent capital acquisition cases up to ₹300 crore, undertaking that this "will shrink the procurement timelines and ensure placement of orders within six months and commencement of deliveries within one year". On 24 June 2025 the Ministry announced thirteen contracts under the Emergency Procurement mechanism worth ₹1,981.90 crore against a sanctioned outlay of ₹2,000 crore for the Indian Army. The Ministry's own Year End Review, published 31 December 2025, puts the same thirteen at ₹1,958.80 crore and does not mention the earlier figure.
claimAtLaunch: Orders placed within six months of a case being progressed, and deliveries commencing within one year — both stated by the DAC as what the delegation would ensure, not as an aspiration.
whatHappened: The power is a per-case ceiling of ₹300 crore. The ₹2,000 crore is a separate sanctioned outlay for one service and one purpose. THESE ARE NOT THE SAME QUANTITY AND ARE NOT ALIGNED HERE: the thirteen contracts' total — on either of the two figures the Ministry gives for it — says nothing about whether any individual case sat under the ₹300 crore ceiling, and neither release states the per-case values. Of the delegation's own two undertakings — orders in six months, deliveries in one year — neither is reported against in anything retrieved. The Year End Review adds that two tranches of emergency procurement were accorded in 2025, that 29 capability development schemes had been contracted, and that a further 16 "are likely to be contracted in Dec 2025".
assessmentNote: Partly, against the objective stated at announcement. The delegation exists, is used, and is used close to its sanctioned limit — that half is delivered and visible. The half that is not is the clock: the DAC undertook specific timelines and no reporting against them was found, so the mechanism's own success criterion is unmeasured five years on. Not too-early: five years is long enough for a six-month and a twelve-month undertaking to be testable, and what is missing is reporting rather than elapsed time.
caseFor: This is a delegation that was used, which is more than can be said for many. Thirteen contracts against a ₹2,000 crore sanction commit between 97.9 and 99.1 per cent of the outlay — 99.1 on the June release's ₹1,981.90 crore, 97.9 on the Year End Review's ₹1,958.80 crore. THE RANGE IS THERE BECAUSE THE TWO MINISTRY TOTALS DIFFER, NOT BECAUSE THE OUTLAY IS UNCERTAIN: the ₹2,000 crore denominator is stated once and identically. On either bound the money was not appropriated and left idle, and the equipment list is specific and operational rather than generic — drone detection and interdiction, low-level lightweight radars, VSHORADS launchers and missiles, loitering munitions, bulletproof jackets, night sights. The 29-schemes-contracted line indicates the mechanism runs beyond this one tranche. And a ₹300 crore ceiling is a genuine constraint: it delegates urgency without delegating major acquisitions.
caseAgainst: An emergency power justified by a border situation in July 2020 was still being used for new sanctions in 2025, which is either a five-year emergency or a fast-track that has become a route. The DAC's own timelines are the natural test of the second reading and nothing reports against them. Oversight is the larger gap: neither release names who reviews an emergency case, what audit attaches, or whether the ₹300 crore ceiling is applied per case or per scheme. And the Ministry cannot state the total consistently — the same thirteen contracts appear at ₹1,981.90 crore in June and ₹1,958.80 crore in the December review.
differentFactsNote: Two Ministry of Defence publications give different totals for what both describe as thirteen Emergency Procurement contracts for the Indian Army's counter-insurgency and counter-terrorism grid: ₹1,981.90 crore in the press release of 24 June 2025 and ₹1,958.80 crore in the Year End Review for 2025, a difference of ₹23.10 crore. Both are T1 and both are the same publisher. The property that makes this unusual is documentable and narrow: THE LATER DOCUMENT ACKNOWLEDGES NO REVISION. The press release of 24 June 2025 gives ₹1,981.90 crore; the Year End Review of 31 December 2025 gives ₹1,958.80 crore, does not contain the figure ₹1,981.90 anywhere, and carries no corrigendum, superseding or earlier-figure language relating to it. A reader meeting either document alone would have no indication the other exists. ORDINARY EXPLANATIONS ARE AVAILABLE and none is ruled out here — a contract revised or descoped after signature, a tax-inclusive against tax-exclusive basis, a differently drawn subset — and ₹23.10 crore is 1.17 per cent of the June total, within the range a single revised contract would produce. The instrument carries both and picks neither. Nothing retrieved distinguishes the possible causes, and this record neither infers one nor asserts that none is available.

unmeasured.why: The delegation was granted on an explicit undertaking about speed, and no reporting against either limb was located. Contract values and counts are published; elapsed time from case initiation to order, and from order to first delivery, are not.

unmeasured.why: Neither the delegation announcement nor the contract announcement names a reviewing authority, an audit requirement, or the unit the ceiling applies to. A per-case ceiling and a per-scheme ceiling are materially different constraints on a thirteen-contract tranche.
unmeasured.wouldFill: The Defence Acquisition Procedure chapter governing emergency procurement, or the DAC minutes of 15 July 2020.

title: Twenty-six Rafale for the Navy, signed government to government, with technology transfer for integrating Indian weapons
summary: In April 2025 the Governments of India and France signed an Inter-Governmental Agreement for 26 Rafale aircraft for the Indian Navy — 22 single-seaters and four twin-seaters — including training, simulator, associated equipment, weapons and performance-based logistics, along with additional equipment for the Indian Air Force's existing Rafale fleet. The agreement includes transfer of technology for the integration of indigenous weapons in India.
claimAtLaunch: Twenty-six aircraft with an associated support package, and transfer of technology for integrating Indian-made weapons onto the platform — the second being the element the Ministry presents as the Aatmanirbhar Bharat content of the deal.
whatHappened: COMMITMENT STATE (a) — NOT YET DUE, AND THE TRIGGER IS NOT NAMED IN THE SOURCE. The agreement was signed in April 2025. No delivery schedule is stated in the material retrieved, so the record cannot give a date by which aircraft are due and does not invent one. What is recorded is the count, the split, the government-to-government form and the technology-transfer term.
assessmentNote: Too-early: the agreement is in force, sixteen months old, and what would settle it — aircraft delivered, weapons actually integrated under the technology transfer — accumulates with time. The absence of a published delivery schedule is recorded as an unmeasured rather than folded into the score, because a missing schedule is a reporting fact and not a reason to judge the acquisition.
caseFor: A government-to-government agreement is the form that carries state-level obligations rather than a vendor's, which matters for a fleet whose support runs decades, and this one buys commonality: the Navy's aircraft share a type with the Air Force's existing fleet, and the package explicitly includes equipment for that fleet. The technology-transfer term is the substantive Aatmanirbharta content and it is specific rather than gestural — integration of indigenous weapons is the capability that determines whether Indian munitions can be carried on the platform at all, and without it the aircraft is a closed system.
caseAgainst: The technology transfer is described and not sized, and integration rights are the kind of term whose value lies entirely in scope: which weapons, on what timetable, with what source-code access, and whether integration can be performed in India without the manufacturer's participation. None of that is stated. Nor is a delivery schedule, so the commitment has no trigger against which non-delivery could ever be recorded — a commitment with no due date cannot move out of state (a) by the passage of time alone. And the strategic argument for a G2G purchase of a Western type sits alongside a fleet still substantially Russian-origin, which is the exposure L-0199 records.

unmeasured.what: The delivery schedule for the 26 Rafale-M aircraft
unmeasured.why: No date, range or rate of delivery appears in the material retrieved. Without one the commitment cannot be resolved beyond state (a), because there is nothing for it to be late against.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A Ministry of Defence statement of the delivery schedule, a Parliamentary answer, or the French government's own account of the contract — a partner government's statement about its own deliveries would be a legitimate second instrument.

unmeasured.what: The scope of the technology transfer for indigenous weapon integration
unmeasured.why: The agreement is stated to include transfer of technology for integrating Indian weapons, and nothing retrieved states which weapons, on what timetable, or whether integration can be carried out in India independently. Integration rights are valuable exactly in proportion to that scope.
unmeasured.wouldFill: The Ministry's own description of the technology-transfer terms, or a Defence Acquisition Council or CCS note on the agreement.

caveat: This record covers the April 2025 Inter-Governmental Agreement for the Navy only. India's earlier Rafale acquisition for the Air Force is not covered: no primary for it was retrieved in this run, and it is not described here on the strength of the 2025 document, which mentions the existing fleet without stating its terms.

revisitTrigger: Re-test when a delivery schedule is published or first delivery occurs, and when the technology-transfer scope is described. Either would move this out of state (a); the first would give the commitment a trigger it currently lacks.

title: The S-400 delivery schedule exists, both governments know it, and neither publishes it — one of them says so on the record
summary: India contracted in 2018 for five S-400 squadrons at US$5.43bn. As at 16 April 2026 two remained undelivered. India's Ministry of Defence, in its Year End Review for 2025, mentions the system twice — a comprehensive annual maintenance contract approved by the Defence Acquisition Council, and "the supply of S-400 systems" as a takeaway from a meeting with the Russian defence minister — and gives no delivery schedule and no delivered count. Russia's ambassador to India, asked directly, confirmed a schedule exists and declined to give it: "We have a mutually agreed timetable, schedule for these deliveries. They will be completed very soon [...] I will not go into the details. The US and the Europeans should know nothing about it."
assessmentNote: A state of the measurement, not a measure. The acquisition has objectives; this record is about what is published against them, and no objective was ever announced about disclosure. Kept separate from L-0199, which covers the CAATSA sanctions exposure of the same acquisition and nothing about deliveries — the two must not be read as one, because a sanctions question and a delivery question have different evidence and different resolutions.
caseFor: Withholding a delivery timetable for an air-defence system is the ordinary practice of every state that operates one, and the ambassador gives the reason in terms: an adversary who knows when a battery arrives knows when it does not. Nothing here suggests the contract is troubled — he states the deliveries are proceeding to a mutually agreed schedule and will finish soon, and the Indian side's own published traces are consistent with an operating system rather than a stalled one, since a comprehensive annual maintenance contract is what a fielded platform needs. The absence is a security judgement, not an accountability failure, and treating every unpublished military figure as concealment would make the category useless.
caseAgainst: The consequence is the same whatever the motive: the largest Russian-origin acquisition in the modern Indian inventory has no public delivery record on either side, so no one outside the two governments can say what has arrived, when, or whether the contract is on time. Every public statement about progress is therefore unfalsifiable — "very soon" has been the position across multiple years — and the instrument's usual recourse, checking one government's account against the other's, is closed because both decline the same quantity. It also matters that the exposure recorded in L-0199 attaches to transactions rather than to deliveries: what is unpublished here is precisely what would let anyone assess how much of that transaction is still running.
differentFactsNote: NOT a differentFacts pair and the reason is specific: the two parties do not give conflicting schedules — neither gives one. And it is not the ordinary single-sided case of L-0191 either, where one party publishes and the other does not. Here BOTH decline the same quantity, and they decline it differently: Russia with an identifiable on-the-record refusal, India with silence. Two absences on one quantity, recorded separately below because their reasons are not the same reason.

unmeasured.what: The S-400 delivery schedule and delivered count, from the Russian side
unmeasured.why: A schedule exists and is mutually agreed — the Russian ambassador said so on 16 April 2026 — and he declined to state it when asked in a broadcast interview: "I will not go into the details [...] this is a sensitive area, which we try to keep under wraps." That is an identifiable refusal to a specific question about a quantity known to exist, which is what distinguishes withheld from not-published.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A Russian Federal Service for Military-Technical Cooperation or Rosoboronexport statement giving delivery dates, or the contract's own schedule.

unmeasured.what: The S-400 delivery schedule and delivered count, from the Indian side
unmeasured.why: The Ministry of Defence's Year End Review for 2025 refers to the system twice without a schedule or a delivered count, and no Indian statement of either was located. No request for it and no refusal of one has been identified, so this is an absence of release rather than a refusal — the narrower category does not apply on the evidence retrieved.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A Ministry of Defence statement or Parliamentary answer giving squadrons delivered and dates, which is the form other acquisition figures take.

caveat: The figure of two squadrons outstanding at 16 April 2026 is TASS's own framing in the same report, not the ambassador's words, and the record carries it as that. Counts of how many had been delivered by earlier dates circulate widely in secondary reporting and are not used here, because no primary for them was retrieved. NOTHING IN THIS RECORD ASSERTS THAT NO SCHEDULE EXISTS: one does, on the ambassador's own statement — what is absent is its publication.

title: The 2016 Rafale agreement bought 36 aircraft off the shelf and dropped 108 that were to be built in India, and the item-wise price is withheld under a 2008 bilateral agreement
summary: An Inter-Governmental Agreement was signed on 23 September 2016 with France for 36 Rafale aircraft in direct fly-away condition, including weapons, long-term maintenance support, simulators, ten years of annual maintenance and associated equipment. It replaced the Medium Multi Role Combat Aircraft proposal for 126 aircraft, of which 18 were to be direct fly-away and 108 licence-manufactured in India. The fly-away component doubled from 18 to 36; the licence-manufactured component went from 108 to none. The Ministry has declined to publish item-wise cost, citing the confidentiality provisions of a 2008 India-France security agreement, and states that an approximate acquisition cost was given to Parliament.
claimAtLaunch: The Ministry's own comparison against the MMRCA proposal, in a Rajya Sabha written reply: "In the IGA, better terms have been achieved in terms of better pricing, better maintenance terms and better delivery schedule." Restated in 2018 as a deal "better in terms of capability, price, equipment, delivery, maintenance, training".
whatHappened: The structural change is the one the announcement does not lead with. MMRCA was 18 fly-away plus 108 built in India under licence; the IGA is 36 fly-away and nothing built in India. Measured on aircraft procured the programme shrank by 90; measured on aircraft to be manufactured domestically it went to zero. The Ministry's stated grounds for the change concern price, maintenance and delivery — the three axes on which it claims improvement — and the domestic-manufacture element is not among the terms it compares.
assessmentNote: Contested, and the reason is that the two sides are arguing about different objectives rather than about the same one. Read as a fighter-acquisition decision the claim is testable in principle on price, maintenance and delivery, and the Ministry asserts improvement on all three. Read as an industrial decision it removed the largest single licence-manufacture commitment in the Indian defence pipeline. Both readings use the same facts, and the record does not choose because the announcement itself does not say which objective governed.
caseFor: MMRCA had already failed as a process — the Ministry's account is that the 126-aircraft procurement "ran aground" and that a personal ministerial veto in 2012 stopped the institutional process while the Air Force's fighter strength was declining. A licence-manufacture commitment that never produces an aircraft delivers no capability and no industry, and 36 in fly-away condition delivered aircraft on a stated schedule where the alternative had delivered none in fourteen years. The fly-away component actually doubled. A government-to-government agreement also carries state-level obligations that a vendor contract does not, which matters over a ten-year maintenance term.
caseAgainst: The industrial content was the part that could not be recovered later, and it was the part dropped. 108 aircraft built in India was the largest transfer-of-manufacture commitment in the pipeline, and nothing in the IGA replaces it — the record shows no licence production, no production line and no equivalent obligation. Against the Aatmanirbharta framing that governs every other record in this arc, the flagship fighter acquisition of the period moved procurement in the opposite direction. And the comparison the Ministry offers cannot be checked: it claims better pricing while declining to publish the price, so the central term of its own defence of the decision is the one term no reader can test.
differentFactsNote: No competing accounts of any fact here — the aircraft counts, the dates and the structure are stated once by the Ministry and not disputed in anything retrieved. The disagreement is about which objective the decision should be judged against, which is a difference of frame rather than of fact.

unmeasured.what: The item-wise cost of the 2016 Rafale contract
unmeasured.why: The Ministry refused it in terms, to an identifiable demand, on 7 February 2018: "The demand that the Government disclose the details and value of the contract for the Rafale aircraft contracted in 2016 is unrealistic", on the ground that item-wise cost would reveal customisations and weapons configurations and "would also come under the ambit of the security agreement signed in 2008". A named refusal to a specific demand, with a stated legal ground, is what distinguishes withheld from not-published. The same statement says an approximate acquisition cost was provided to Parliament; that figure was not retrieved in this run and no price is stated in this record.
unmeasured.wouldFill: The Parliamentary answer carrying the approximate acquisition cost, or the Comptroller and Auditor General's report on the acquisition, which was tabled and would carry the audited comparison.

unmeasured.what: Whether any domestic-manufacture obligation replaced the 108 licence-built aircraft
unmeasured.why: The IGA is described as covering weapons, maintenance, simulators and associated equipment, and nothing retrieved states an offset or transfer-of-manufacture obligation that substitutes for the licence production the MMRCA proposal carried. Absence of a statement is not a statement of absence, and the record says only that none was located.
unmeasured.wouldFill: The offset schedule for the 2016 IGA, or a Ministry statement of offset obligations discharged against it.

caveat: No price figure appears in this record. The Ministry states that an approximate acquisition cost was given to Parliament, so a public figure exists; it was not retrieved here and none is quoted, inferred or reconstructed. Nothing in this record asserts that the contract value is unknown to Parliament — only that it was not retrieved in this run and that item-wise cost is withheld.
