title: The India-UK trade agreement is in force, and the two headline concessions are not the same measurement: 99 per cent of India's exports by value against 24.5 per cent of Britain's on day one
summary: The India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement entered into force on 15 July 2026, alongside a Double Contribution Convention on social security whose exemption period was raised from three years to five. CETA was concluded on 6 May 2025 after fourteen negotiating rounds and signed in London on 24 July 2025. The UK gives zero-duty access to nearly 99 per cent of India's exports, covering almost 100 per cent of the trade value. India offers concessions on 89.5 per cent of its tariff lines, covering 91 per cent of UK exports — but only 24.5 per cent of UK export VALUE receives immediate duty-free access, the rest being phased.
claimAtLaunch: The India-UK Roadmap 2030, adopted in May 2021 alongside the Enhanced Trade Partnership, set the goal of doubling bilateral trade to US$100bn by 2030. CETA is presented as the instrument, and as balancing liberalisation against the protection of sensitive sectors through exclusions and phased reductions.
whatHappened: COMMITMENT STATE (a) — NOT YET DUE, TRIGGER NAMED: 2030, for the US$100bn doubling. The agreement is three weeks old at the date of this record and nothing about the trade outcome is testable. What is recorded is the structure, and one feature of it that the published framing does not draw out. THE TWO CONCESSIONS ARE MEASURED DIFFERENTLY AND ARE ROUTINELY QUOTED SIDE BY SIDE. Britain's is stated as a share of India's exports AND of trade value, at zero duty, with no phasing mentioned: 99 per cent of exports, almost 100 per cent of value. India's headline is a share of TARIFF LINES — 89.5 per cent — and the value figure attached to it is 24.5 per cent immediate. A line count and a value share are different quantities, and an immediate concession and a phased one are different commitments; 99 against 89.5 compares neither like with like.
assessmentNote: Too-early in its strict sense: the agreement is in force, the obstacle is elapsed time, and the evidence that would settle it — trade flows under the new schedule — accumulates. Three weeks is not a basis for any judgement about outcomes. The record exists now because the terms are fixed now and the phasing schedule is the thing most easily forgotten once headline percentages enter circulation.
caseFor: The asymmetry runs in India's favour and that is the plain reading of the numbers. India's exports get near-total immediate zero-duty access to a high-income market; Britain's get a line-count concession most of whose value arrives later. For a country whose standing complaint about trade agreements is that they open its market faster than they open others', this one is drawn the other way, and the phasing is the mechanism that does it. The services and mobility side is substantive rather than decorative — the Double Contribution Convention's exemption period went from three years to five, which is a direct cost saving for Indian professionals posted to the UK, and the Ministry describes the UK's services commitments as among the most ambitious it has offered in any FTA. Fourteen rounds and a fourteen-month gap between signature and entry into force also indicate ratification was done properly rather than announced early.
caseAgainst: The comparison the release invites is not one the figures support, and the mismatch is systematic rather than incidental: the favourable side is quoted by value and the concessionary side by line count, which is the arrangement that makes any agreement look most favourable. 89.5 per cent of lines is not 89.5 per cent of anything a reader cares about, and the number that answers the question a reader is actually asking — how much of Britain's exports get in duty-free now — is 24.5 per cent, which appears once and not in the headline. The doubling target is also inherited rather than set by this agreement: US$100bn by 2030 was adopted in 2021, and a target restated at entry into force with five years left and no interim milestone is not a commitment this instrument can test until the year it falls due.
differentFactsNote: No competing accounts of any figure — every number here is India's own and none is disputed in anything retrieved. The finding is that two of them measure different things and are presented as comparable, which is a framing question rather than a factual dispute. Recorded here rather than as a dispute record for that reason.

unmeasured.why: The published material gives the day-one figure (24.5 per cent of UK export value) and the eventual line coverage (89.5 per cent of lines) and nothing between them. Without the schedule, the pace at which India's market opens is not measurable, and the two published figures cannot be reconciled into a single trajectory.

unmeasured.why: The target was set in the India-UK Roadmap 2030 and is restated at entry into force. Nothing retrieved names a year-by-year path or a mid-point figure, so the commitment is untestable until the terminal year — the same shape recorded for TEPA's investment objective in L-0194.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A Roadmap 2030 progress report, or a Ministry statement of interim trade targets.

title: The India-EU agreement is concluded but not in force, and this time both sides published the same two measurements — 90.7 per cent of India's export value duty-free at once against 30.6 per cent of the EU's
summary: The Prime Minister and the President of the European Commission announced the conclusion of India-EU Free Trade Agreement negotiations at the 16th India-EU Summit on 27 January 2026, after a re-launch of talks in 2022. The EU eliminates duties on about 70.4 per cent of its tariff lines at entry into force, covering 90.7 per cent of India's export value, with a further 20.3 per cent of products phased; its total offer is almost 97 per cent of lines and more than 99 per cent of trade value. India gives immediate duty-free access on about 49.6 per cent of its tariff lines covering 30.6 per cent of trade value, with 39.5 per cent of lines and 63.1 per cent of value phased over five, seven or ten years; India's total offer is around 92.1 per cent of lines and 97.5 per cent of value.
claimAtLaunch: A balanced, modern and rules-based partnership delivering, on the Ministry's statement, preferential entry for over 99 per cent of Indian exports and zero duty at entry into force on almost US$33bn of exports in labour-intensive sectors — textiles, leather, marine products, gems and jewellery — that currently face duties of up to 10 per cent. On services, the EU opens 144 subsectors to India and India opens 102 to the EU.
whatHappened: COMMITMENT STATE (a) — NOT YET DUE, AND THE TRIGGER IS A NAMED CONDITION RATHER THAN A DATE. The FAQ states the mechanism precisely: the agreement enters into force "on the first day of the second month following the date on which India and the EU exchange written notifications confirming completion of their respective internal legal procedures, or on any other date mutually agreed". So conclusion of negotiations is not signature and is not entry into force, and no date exists for either — but unlike the Rafale-M agreement in L-0201 there IS a stated trigger, and it can be observed when it occurs. Nothing in the schedule runs until it does.
assessmentNote: Too-early: negotiations are concluded, the obstacle is elapsed time and the procedural steps time carries. Not awaiting-adjudication — the exchange of notifications is an act of the parties themselves, not a decision by any body outside them.
caseFor: The disclosure is the best in this arc and that deserves saying plainly. Both sides' offers are published on BOTH bases — lines and trade value — and split into immediate and phased, which is exactly what the India-UK release did not do and what makes an asymmetry visible instead of buried. On substance the asymmetry runs India's way at entry into force by 60.1 percentage points of value, the labour-intensive sectors that employ most are the ones getting immediate zero duty on around US$33bn of exports, and India's own opening is deliberately staged over five to ten years, which is the protection its sensitive sectors were promised. Concluding with the EU after a decade of stalled attempts is a substantive outcome whatever the schedule.
caseAgainst: Concluded is not signed and signed is not in force, and the difference is not procedural detail — nothing in the schedule binds until notifications are exchanged, and no date exists for that. The headline that circulates is "over 99 per cent of Indian exports", which is the eventual figure; the day-one figure for India's exports is 90.7 per cent of value and for the EU's is 30.6 per cent, and only the second tells a reader what changes when the agreement starts. India's phasing runs to ten years, which is longer than most governments last. And the published components do not add up to the published totals on any of the three splits, so the schedules cannot be reconstructed from what has been released.
differentFactsNote: No competing accounts: every figure is from Indian government publications and none is disputed in anything retrieved. The asymmetry between the two offers is a property of the agreement, not a disagreement about it.

unmeasured.what: The residual between the published immediate and phased shares and the published totals, on all three splits
unmeasured.why: The components do not sum to the stated totals and no third category is described. EU lines: 70.4 immediate plus 20.3 phased is 90.7, against a stated total of almost 97 — a gap of about 6.3 points. India lines: 49.6 plus 39.5 is 89.1 against 92.1 — a gap of 3.0. India value: 30.6 plus 63.1 is 93.7 against 97.5 — a gap of 3.8. Something is conceded that is neither immediate elimination nor phased elimination — tariff-rate quotas and partial reductions are the ordinary candidates — and nothing retrieved names it. The gaps are recorded rather than reconciled.
unmeasured.wouldFill: The agreement's tariff schedule annexes, or a Ministry statement of the concession categories and their shares.

unmeasured.what: The date of signature and the date of exchange of notifications
unmeasured.why: Conclusion of negotiations was announced on 27 January 2026. The entry-into-force rule is stated as a condition, not a date, and neither a signature date nor a notification-exchange date appears in anything retrieved.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A Ministry announcement of signature, or of the exchange of written notifications, either of which starts the clock the FAQ describes.

caveat: Two coincidences of arithmetic in the published figures are noted so a reader does not take either for a relationship. First, the EU's immediate and phased line shares sum to 90.7, which is also the figure given for the share of India's export VALUE covered by the immediate tranche — the same number attached to two different quantities, a line count and a value share, related by no arithmetic. Second, India's 2024-25 bilateral goods trade is given as US$136.54bn against exports of US$75.85bn and imports of US$60.68bn, which sum to 136.53; the total is computed on unrounded values and the 0.01 is a rounding artefact, not a discrepancy.

revisitTrigger: Re-test on signature, and on the exchange of written notifications — the second starts the clock the FAQ describes and is what moves this out of state (a). If the tariff schedule annexes are published, the undescribed residual above becomes measurable at the same time.

title: The Maldives currency swap is an eligibility with a size and an expiry, and nothing published says how much of it was drawn
summary: The Reserve Bank of India entered a Currency Swap Agreement with the Maldives Monetary Authority on 7 October 2024 in New Delhi, under the SAARC Currency Swap Framework 2024-27. The MMA is eligible for US$400 million under the US Dollar/Euro Swap Window and INR 30 billion under the INR Swap Window. The agreement is valid until 18 June 2027. The framework itself has operated since 15 November 2012 and is described by the RBI as a backstop for short-term foreign exchange liquidity or balance-of-payments stress "till longer term arrangements are made".
claimAtLaunch: The framework's stated purpose, in the RBI's own words: a backstop line of funding for short-term foreign exchange liquidity requirements or short-term balance of payments stress, pending longer-term arrangements. No objective is stated for the Maldives agreement specifically beyond membership of that framework.
whatHappened: WHAT IS PUBLISHED IS AN ELIGIBILITY, NOT A DRAWING. The agreement establishes what the MMA may access; nothing retrieved states how much, if any, was drawn, when, or whether it has been repaid. Those are different quantities and the record does not treat the first as evidence of the second. The agreement runs to 18 June 2027 — a date, not a condition — so it is testable on its own terms when it expires.
assessmentNote: A facility, not a measure with an announced outcome. The framework states a purpose but the bilateral agreement announces no target against which it could have worked or failed, and a swap line that is never drawn is not thereby a failure — an unused backstop may be doing exactly what a backstop does. Scoring it would require an objective neither party stated.
caseFor: This is the instrument doing what it was built for. The framework has existed since 2012 and is available to SAARC members on standing terms rather than being improvised per crisis, which is what makes it a backstop rather than a rescue. Two windows in different currencies give the counterparty a genuine choice, and the INR window is the concrete form of rupee internationalisation rather than a slogan about it. The terms are published in full — date, both window sizes, expiry — which is more than most bilateral financial arrangements disclose.
caseAgainst: The published figure is a ceiling and is routinely read as a transfer. US$400 million is what the MMA MAY draw, and whether any of it moved is not published by either party; a reader meeting the number in isolation would reasonably take it for support extended rather than support available. The framework's own language concedes that it is provisional — funding "till longer term arrangements are made" — so the agreement describes a bridge without stating what it bridges to. And the expiry of 18 June 2027 is common to the framework rather than negotiated for the Maldives, so it carries no information about the specific relationship.

unmeasured.what: How much of the swap was drawn by the Maldives Monetary Authority, when, and whether it has been repaid
unmeasured.why: The RBI publishes the agreement and its ceilings, not drawings under it. Nothing retrieved from either the RBI or the MMA states utilisation. Eligibility and utilisation are different quantities, and the published number is the first.
unmeasured.wouldFill: RBI's Weekly Statistical Supplement or Annual Report if either discloses SAARC swap drawings, or a Maldives Monetary Authority statement of its own external liabilities.

caveat: The two windows are stated in different currencies — US$400 million and INR 30 billion — and this record does not convert between them or add them. The RBI's announcement gives no exchange rate and no combined figure, and the SAARC framework's own design operates windows within an overall facility size that this announcement does not state.

sources.name: Reserve Bank of India, "RBI enters into Currency Swap Agreement with Maldives Monetary Authority", Press Release 2024-2025/1241, 7 October 2024 — the agreement date, both window sizes, the 18 June 2027 expiry, and the SAARC framework's operation since 15 November 2012 with its stated purpose

revisitTrigger: Re-test on 18 June 2027 when the agreement expires, and earlier if any drawing is published. Expiry without a published drawing would leave the facility's use unmeasured for its whole life, which is itself the finding.

title: Punatsangchhu-II exported power to India for nearly seven months before the tariff protocol was signed, and no tariff figure has been published for either period
summary: The 1020 MW Punatsangchhu-II Hydroelectric Project in Bhutan commenced export of surplus power to India on 19 September 2025 "at a mutually agreed starting tariff", and was jointly inaugurated by the Prime Minister of India and the King of Bhutan on 11 November 2025. The Tariff Protocol for the project was signed on 9 April 2026, during the Union Power Minister's visit to Bhutan, alongside a Methodology for Reactive Energy Accounting of reactive power exchange. Indo-Bhutan hydropower cooperation is dated by the Ministry to 1961, with an agreement on hydroelectric power cooperation in 2006.
claimAtLaunch: The Ministry's framing at the signing: another step in mutually beneficial hydropower cooperation, within an enhanced bilateral institutional framework mechanism covering non-hydro energy, cross-border transmission, project financing, capacity building and institutional partnerships. No tariff, revenue or export-volume target is stated for the project in anything retrieved.
whatHappened: THE POWER MOVED BEFORE THE PRICE WAS SETTLED, AND THE PRICE IS NOT PUBLISHED IN EITHER PERIOD. Export began on 19 September 2025 at what the Ministry calls "a mutually agreed starting tariff" — a phrase that concedes an interim arrangement — and the Tariff Protocol was signed on 9 April 2026, six months and three weeks later. In between, on 3 February 2026, the Bhutanese Energy Minister and the Union Power Minister were still deliberating "the commercial optimization of power output" from the project, which places the commercial terms unsettled more than four months after power began flowing. Neither the starting tariff nor the protocol tariff appears in anything retrieved.
assessmentNote: Scored on delivery and on delivery only: the project was built, commissioned and is exporting, which is what a joint hydropower project is for, and the two governments inaugurated it jointly. The commercial terms are NOT scored here and cannot be — no tariff is published for either period and no revenue or volume target was announced against which the arrangement could be judged. A reader should take this score as saying the electricity flows, not that the deal is good.
caseFor: The plant exists and is exporting, which is more than most of the pipeline can say — the companion project at Punatsangchhu-I was still awaiting commissioning in February 2026 after far longer. Beginning export on an interim tariff rather than waiting for the protocol is the choice that gets power onto the grid earliest, and Bhutan is paid from the first unit rather than from the signature. The 9 April 2026 signings are substantive rather than ceremonial: a tariff protocol and a reactive-energy accounting methodology are the two instruments a cross-border interconnection actually needs to settle accounts and hold the grid stable. The institutional framework agreed at the same time gives the relationship a standing review mechanism instead of ministerial visits.
caseAgainst: The sequence inverts the ordinary protection. Power flowed for six months and three weeks on an interim price, which means the smaller party's revenue for that period was determined by an arrangement neither government has published and neither parliament has seen. "Commercial optimization" was still under deliberation in February 2026, so the terms were not merely unpublished but unfinished while the asset ran. And the protocol's signature does not close the disclosure: no tariff figure exists in the public record for the interim period or the settled one, so nothing about the price — whether it rose, fell or was applied retrospectively — can be checked by anyone outside the two ministries.

unmeasured.what: The interim tariff applied from 19 September 2025, and the tariff set by the Protocol signed 9 April 2026
unmeasured.why: The Ministry states that export began "at a mutually agreed starting tariff" and that a Tariff Protocol was later signed, without giving either figure. The numbers exist — an interim tariff that power was sold at is a number both parties hold, and a signed protocol contains its rate — so this is not-published rather than not-collected. No identifiable refusal was located, which is what keeps it short of withheld.
unmeasured.wouldFill: The text of the Tariff Protocol, a Central Electricity Regulatory Commission filing on the import, or a Parliamentary answer stating the rate.

unmeasured.what: Whether the Protocol's tariff was applied retrospectively to the interim period, and how much energy was exported before it was signed
unmeasured.why: Nothing retrieved states the Protocol's effective date or whether it reopens the interim sales, and no export volume is published for the period from 19 September 2025. Without both, the value transferred under the interim arrangement cannot be bounded even approximately.
unmeasured.wouldFill: The Protocol's commencement clause, or Ministry of Power / Central Electricity Authority monthly cross-border exchange data for the Bhutan interconnections.

caveat: The 1020 MW figure is the project's installed capacity as stated by the Ministry, not a measure of energy exported, and this record derives no export quantity from it. The interval between 19 September 2025 and 9 April 2026 is stated as six months and three weeks and is an elapsed period between two published dates; it is not a claim about how long any tariff negotiation took, which is not published.

sources.name: Ministry of Power, "Union Minister Shri Manohar Lal Arrives in Bhutan; Reaffirms India-Bhutan Partnership on Clean Energy and Sustainable Development", PIB, 9 April 2026 — the Tariff Protocol and Reactive Energy Accounting Methodology signings, the 1020 MW capacity, the 11 November 2025 joint inauguration, the 19 September 2025 commencement of export "at a mutually agreed starting tariff", and the enhanced bilateral institutional framework mechanism

Ministry of Power, "India and Bhutan to Strengthen Cooperation in the Power Sector", PIB, 3 February 2026 — the deliberation on "commercial optimization of power output" from Punatsangchhu-II, the call for early commissioning of Punatsangchhu-I (1200 MW), cooperation dated to 1961 with the 2006 hydroelectric power agreement, and the assessment of cross-border transmission links till 2040

revisitTrigger: Re-test if any tariff figure is published for either period, or if cross-border exchange volumes for the Bhutan interconnections are released. Either would make the value of the interim arrangement measurable for the first time; without them it stays unmeasurable however long the plant runs.

title: The Ministry of Power's account of neighbourhood cooperation lists capacity without commissioning status and agreements without dates, and two rows of the same column are demonstrably in different states
summary: A Lok Sabha written reply of 2 April 2026 set out India's power-sector cooperation with Bhutan, Nepal, Bangladesh, Myanmar and Sri Lanka in two tables. Table-1 lists Memoranda of Understanding and agreements by the parties to them. Table-2 lists thirteen generation projects with an installed-capacity column — six in Nepal, six in Bhutan, one in Bangladesh — and thirty cross-border transmission links: fifteen with Nepal, nine with Bhutan, three with Bangladesh, two with Myanmar and one with Sri Lanka.
claimAtLaunch: No objective is announced. The reply is a description of engagement — that the Ministry and its public sector enterprises "engage with neighbouring countries ... to strengthen cooperation in the power sector" — and states no target, date or outcome for any project or agreement listed.
whatHappened: WHAT THE TABLES OMIT IS THE COLUMN THAT WOULD MAKE THEM READABLE. Table-2 gives installed capacity in megawatts for every generation project under one heading, with no column for commissioning status, and the same for thirty transmission links. That the omission is load-bearing rather than pedantic can be shown from the Ministry's own releases in the same period: Punatsangchhu-II (1020 MW) commenced export to India on 19 September 2025, while Punatsangchhu-I (1200 MW) was the subject of a call for "early commissioning" on 3 February 2026. One row is exporting and one is not built, and they sit adjacent in the same column under the same unit. Table-1 has the parallel defect on the agreements side: it names the parties to each instrument and nothing else — no title, no date, no term, no status — so it establishes that agreements exist without disclosing what any of them says.
assessmentNote: No-objective in its strict sense: the reply announces no target, date or outcome for any project or agreement it lists, so there is nothing against which it could have worked or failed. What it establishes is what can and cannot be measured from the Ministry's own account. Recorded so that the capacity column is not later read as a stock of operating plant, which is the reading its presentation invites and the one it does not support.
caseFor: The reply discloses more than it was obliged to and more than the equivalent answers in most sectors. Thirty named transmission links with voltages, circuit configurations and both endpoints is a genuinely specific inventory, and naming every counterparty enterprise — NHPC, NTPC, NVVN, SJVN, Power Grid — lets a reader trace any of them further. The tripartite Nepal-India-Bangladesh arrangement among NEA, NVVN and the Bangladesh Power Development Board is disclosed at all, which is not obvious for a three-country transaction. And a written answer is a schedule, not a report; the question asked what exists, and the tables answer it.
caseAgainst: A capacity column is read as capacity, and a reader who adds this one gets a number that does not exist. Built plant and unbuilt plant are set out identically in megawatts, so the shared unit conceals the difference rather than exposing it — the reader must already know which rows are real to use the table, which is the knowledge the table was supposed to supply. The same is true of the transmission list, where a 1000 MW India-Sri Lanka HVDC bipole appears beside links that have carried power for decades. Table-1 is weaker still: a list of agreements identified only by their signatories cannot be checked, dated, or matched to any project in Table-2, and it discloses the existence of obligations while withholding every one of their terms.

unmeasured.what: The commissioning status and commissioning date of each of the thirteen generation projects and thirty transmission links
unmeasured.why: No status column appears in either table, and the reply describes them all under the single heading of details of projects. The Ministry necessarily holds commissioning dates for assets its own enterprises built, so the information exists and was not released in this answer.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A Ministry of Power or Central Electricity Authority statement of commissioning dates by project, or a subsequent Parliamentary answer carrying a status column.

unmeasured.what: The date, title, term and current status of each agreement in Table-1
unmeasured.why: Table-1 identifies every instrument by its parties alone. Whether any is still in force, when it was executed, and what it obliges either side to do are not stated. The instruments exist and are held by the executing bodies, so this is not-published; nothing retrieved records a request for them being refused, which is what keeps it short of withheld.
unmeasured.wouldFill: The texts of the MoUs, or a Parliamentary answer listing them with dates and terms.

unmeasured.what: Energy actually exchanged over any of the thirty links
unmeasured.why: The tables list infrastructure, not flows. Capacity and connection are what is published; how much electricity moved in either direction, over what period, is not stated anywhere in the reply.
unmeasured.wouldFill: Central Electricity Authority cross-border exchange data, or a Parliamentary answer on import and export volumes by link.

caveat: This record does not sum the installed-capacity column and no total is stated, because its entries are not in the same state and the shared megawatt unit does not make them commensurable. The counts given here — thirteen generation projects and thirty transmission links, distributed fifteen, nine, three, two and one — are counts of rows as printed, not of the source's serial numbers, which contain a defect: the Nepal transmission list skips serial 13 and gives serial 14 twice, and the two errors cancel so that the final serial reaches 30 correctly. The count is stated from the rows for that reason.

Ministry of Power, "India and Bhutan to Strengthen Cooperation in the Power Sector", PIB, 3 February 2026 — the call for early commissioning of Punatsangchhu-I, which with the 19 September 2025 export commencement of Punatsangchhu-II establishes that two rows of the same capacity column are in different states

revisitTrigger: Re-test if a later Parliamentary answer on the same subject carries a commissioning-status column or dates for the Table-1 agreements. The India-Sri Lanka HVDC bipole is the single most informative row to watch, because it is the one link in the list for which no operating history exists at all.

title: The decision to fence the entire 1,643 km Myanmar border was announced with a starting position of 10 km and no completion date, and the Ministry's own year-end review for that year gives no progress figure at all
summary: On 6 February 2024 the Union Home Minister announced, in a post on X reproduced as a PIB release, that the government had decided to construct a fence along the entire 1,643 kilometre Indo-Myanmar border, with a paved patrol track alongside. The same announcement gave the starting position: 10 km fenced in Moreh, Manipur; two Hybrid Surveillance System pilot projects under execution covering 1 km each in Arunachal Pradesh and Manipur; and fence works of approximately 20 km in Manipur approved, with work to start soon. No completion date was stated.
claimAtLaunch: "The Modi government is committed to building impenetrable borders. It has decided to construct a fence along the entire 1643-kilometer-long Indo-Myanmar border. To facilitate better surveillance, a patrol track along the border will also be paved." The commitment is to a total length. No date, no phasing, no annual target and no cost accompany it.
whatHappened: A TOTAL WITHOUT A DATE CANNOT BECOME DUE. The commitment names a quantity — the entire 1,643 km — and no time by which it is to exist, so it falls outside all three commitment states this instrument uses: it is not (a) not-yet-due with a named trigger, because no trigger is named; it cannot reach (b) due-and-undelivered, because it can never fall due; and it cannot reach (c) abandoned without evidence of abandonment, which nothing supplies. WHAT CAN BE CHECKED IS WHETHER PROGRESS IS REPORTED, AND IT IS NOT. The Ministry of Home Affairs' own Year End Review 2024 — its comprehensive account of the year in which the decision was taken — contains the figure 1,643 nowhere, uses the words fence and fenced nowhere, and uses fencing once: in a recommendation that demographic data along the border "should be mapped to help in fencing the border and stopping infiltration". That is a proposal, not a progress report.
assessmentNote: No-objective in the sense this instrument uses it: an objective is a target that can be failed. A total length with no date can never be due and therefore can never be undelivered, so it names a destination rather than a commitment. This is not a judgement that the fence is unbuilt or that the decision was insincere — it is that the announcement as made cannot be scored against itself at any future moment, and no later Ministry publication retrieved here supplies the date or the progress that would change that.
caseFor: The decision itself is specific where it matters most: a named total length, a named border, and a stated intention to pave a patrol track, which is the element that makes a fence patrollable rather than ornamental. Announcing the starting position in the same breath — 10 km already fenced, two pilots under execution, 20 km approved — is more candid than the announcement required, and it means the base against which any later figure would be read was published on day one rather than reconstructed afterwards. Fencing a 1,643 km border across Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur and Mizoram is genuinely hard terrain, and refusing to name a date may be honesty about that rather than evasion.
caseAgainst: The announcement's structure makes it permanently unfalsifiable, and that is a choice, not an accident. Every element that would let a reader test it later — a completion year, an annual target, a cost, a phasing plan — is absent, while the element that makes it quotable, the 1,643 km total, is present. The Ministry then published a year-end review of the very year the decision was taken which does not carry the total, does not carry a progress figure, and mentions fencing only in a recommendation about demographic mapping. A commitment that names no date and is not reported against in the responsible ministry's own annual account is one no reader can hold anyone to, however long it stands.

unmeasured.what: The date by which the 1,643 km is to be fenced
unmeasured.why: Neither the announcement nor the Ministry's Year End Review 2024 states a completion date, a phasing schedule or an annual target. This is not a figure held and unreleased: a date that was never set does not exist to be published, which is what distinguishes it from the progress figure below.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A Ministry of Home Affairs statement of a target year or phasing plan, or a Parliamentary answer giving one.

unmeasured.what: How much of the 1,643 km has been fenced since 6 February 2024
unmeasured.why: The Ministry of Home Affairs and its executing agencies necessarily hold current progress for works they commission, so the figure exists. It is absent from the place it would naturally appear: the Ministry's Year End Review 2024, checked in full, carries no fencing length, no reference to the 1,643 km total, and no progress statement of any kind. Absence from the responsible ministry's own annual account is what makes this not-published rather than merely not-retrieved.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A Parliamentary answer stating kilometres fenced to date, or a Ministry of Home Affairs Annual Report figure for the Indo-Myanmar border.

caveat: No share is computed here. The announcement's four quantities are in four different states — 10 km fenced, 2 km under execution as pilots, approximately 20 km approved, 1,643 km intended — and only the first is completed work, so adding any of them or dividing them into the total would produce a figure that describes nothing. The record therefore states the 10 km and the 1,643 km side by side and derives no percentage from them. The 23rd India-Myanmar National Level Meeting readout of 8 July 2026 does not mention fencing; that is recorded as a fact about the readout and is not evidence of abandonment, since absence of news is not evidence that a commitment was dropped.

Ministry of Home Affairs, "Ministry of Home Affairs: Year End Review 2024", PIB — checked in full for fencing progress: the total 1,643 does not appear, the words fence and fenced do not appear, and fencing appears only in the recommendation that demographic data along the India-Myanmar border be mapped "to help in fencing the border and stopping infiltration"

Ministry of Home Affairs, "23rd National Level Meeting between India and Myanmar concludes in New Delhi", PIB, 8 July 2026 — the most recent bilateral home-ministry readout retrieved, covering border security, transnational crime, the Kaladan project and the trilateral highway, and not mentioning fencing

title: The Ministry that announced the Free Movement Regime would be scrapped does not own the instrument, and its own text says it recommended a suspension while another ministry was still in the process
summary: On 8 February 2024 the Ministry of Home Affairs announced that the Free Movement Regime between India and Myanmar — which permitted local residents on either side to cross the border without a visa — would be scrapped, to ensure internal security and to maintain the demographic structure of India's North Eastern States bordering Myanmar. The release reproduces a post on X by the Union Home Minister, whose text states that the Ministry of External Affairs "is currently in the process of scrapping it" and that MHA "has recommended the immediate suspension of the FMR".
claimAtLaunch: That the FMR between India and Myanmar be scrapped, on two stated grounds: the internal security of the country, and the maintenance of the demographic structure of India's North Eastern States bordering Myanmar. No date of effect, no notification number, no replacement arrangement and no test of completion accompany it.
whatHappened: THREE DIFFERENT ACTS ARE COMPRESSED INTO ONE ANNOUNCEMENT, AND THE HEADLINE REPORTS ONLY THE STRONGEST. The quoted text contains a decision by MHA that the regime "be scrapped", a statement that MEA "is currently in the process of scrapping it", and a recommendation by MHA of "the immediate suspension". The instrument belongs to the Ministry of External Affairs; what the Ministry of Home Affairs did on its own authority was decide a position and recommend. The headline — "MHA decides to scrap" — reports the act of the ministry that cannot perform it. WHETHER IT WAS PERFORMED IS NOT RECORDED WHERE IT WOULD BE. The Ministry's Year End Review 2024 restates this same announcement in two separate sections, word for word, more than ten months later, and adds nothing: no notification, no date of effect, no replacement regime, no statement that the scrapping was completed.
assessmentNote: Scored on what the announcing ministry actually committed itself to, which is a recommendation and a stated position — neither of which carries a completion test, a date or an instrument. MHA set no objective against which MHA could be measured. This is expressly NOT a finding that the FMR survives or that it was scrapped; that question is unmeasured below, and the record names both where it would be recorded and why this run cannot settle it.
caseFor: The grounds were stated plainly rather than left to be inferred, and both are legitimate subjects of the Ministry's responsibility: internal security, and the demographic composition of border districts during a period of acute instability across the frontier. Announcing that MEA was already in process is a disclosure of the actual division of authority rather than a concealment of it — the release could simply have said the regime was scrapped and did not. Recommending immediate suspension while the formal instrument was unwound is the mechanism that closes the gap between decision and notification, and for a border regime during an insurgency that gap is the whole risk.
caseAgainst: The distinction the text preserves is the one the headline destroys, and it is the headline that circulates. A recommendation by one ministry to another is a lesser thing than a decision, and presenting it as "MHA decides to scrap" attributes to the announcing body an authority the same paragraph concedes it does not hold. The evidentiary basis is a social-media post: no notification, no order number, no date of effect appears in the release or anywhere retrieved. And the Ministry's own year-end review, published more than ten months later, reproduces the announcement twice without adding a single fact about its execution — so the most recent MHA account of the matter is the announcement itself, restated.

unmeasured.what: Whether the Free Movement Regime was in fact scrapped or suspended, by what instrument, and with effect from what date
unmeasured.why: The instrument belongs to the Ministry of External Affairs, and the announcement states only that MEA was "in the process". Nothing retrieved from the Ministry of Home Affairs records completion: its Year End Review 2024 restates the February announcement in two sections and adds nothing. MEA's own publications could not be retrieved in this environment at all — its press-release path returns an HTTP 200 serving a JavaScript shell, confirmed on two separate paths this cycle — so this record CANNOT distinguish between MEA having published nothing and MEA having published something unreachable here. The classification records the absence from MHA's account, which was checked; it does not assert an absence from MEA's, which was not.
unmeasured.wouldFill: The Ministry of External Affairs notification or gazette instrument, or a Parliamentary answer stating the FMR's current status and date of effect.

unmeasured.what: What arrangement, if any, replaced the Free Movement Regime for border residents
unmeasured.why: The announcement states what is to be removed and nothing about what governs local crossing afterwards. No replacement scheme, pass system or transitional arrangement appears in anything retrieved, including the Year End Review 2024.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A Ministry of Home Affairs or Ministry of External Affairs statement of the arrangement now governing local border crossing, or the standard operating procedure issued to the Assam Rifles.

caveat: This record makes no claim about whether the Free Movement Regime is in force today. The retrieval limit is the reason and is stated rather than worked around: the ministry that owns the instrument publishes through a route that cannot be read in this environment, so silence on that side is uninformative here and is not treated as evidence. What is established is confined to what the Ministry of Home Affairs published and to what its own year-end review does and does not contain. The 23rd India-Myanmar National Level Meeting readout of 8 July 2026 does not mention the Free Movement Regime; as with the fencing record, that is a fact about the readout and not evidence that the commitment was dropped.

title: India's electricity exports to Bangladesh were published as a measured four-year series up to January 2023 and have not been published since, and the Ministry of Power's own account of 2025 does not mention Bangladesh at all
summary: A Parliamentary reply of 28 March 2023 published net cross-border electricity flows sourced from the Central Electricity Authority, by counterparty and financial year, in Million Units. India's exports to Bangladesh were 6,987.94 in 2019-20, 7,551.99 in 2020-21, 7,301.74 in 2021-22 and 7,234.08 in 2022-23 up to January 2023. An earlier reply of 19 March 2020 gave 6,168.14 for 2019-20 as on January 2020. No later series was retrieved: the Ministry of Power's Year End Review 2025, published 16 January 2026, does not mention Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, exports or cross-border trade anywhere in its 49,271 characters, and the comprehensive Lok Sabha reply of 2 April 2026 recorded at L-0208 lists infrastructure without flows.
claimAtLaunch: None stated. Both replies are answers to questions rather than announcements, and neither sets a target for cross-border trade, a volume to be reached, or a schedule for reporting.
whatHappened: THE QUANTITY IS COLLECTED, WAS PUBLISHED, AND HAS STOPPED APPEARING. The 2023 series is attributed to the Central Electricity Authority, which compiles it continuously; nothing suggests collection ceased. What changed is disclosure. The most recent comprehensive account of neighbourhood power cooperation lists thirteen generation projects and thirty transmission links and no volume over any of them; the Ministry's own year-end review of 2025 does not mention the neighbourhood at all. THE PUBLISHED SERIES ALSO SETS A PARTIAL YEAR BESIDE FULL ONES. The top row, 7,234.08, covers ten months to January 2023; the three rows beneath it cover twelve. Read down the column the figure appears flat against 7,301.74 for the full year before it, and that reading is unavailable — the periods differ.
assessmentNote: No target, volume or reporting commitment is announced in either reply, so there is nothing that could have worked or failed. What the record establishes is what is measurable about this relationship and when it stopped being published, which is the precondition for scoring anything else about it later.
caseFor: The series is better disclosure than most of this arc contains, and it deserves saying. It is attributed to a named compiler rather than floated unsourced, it gives four consecutive years on a consistent unit, it covers every land neighbour, and it marks direction per cell rather than assuming one — which is what lets a reader see that India moved from exporting 1,921.09 Million Units to Nepal in 2021-22 to importing 488.96 in the ten months following, a reversal that a one-directional table would have hidden. The two replies are also consistent with each other once their cut-offs are read: 6,987.94 for the full year 2019-20 against 6,168.14 as on January 2020 leaves 819.80 Million Units in the remainder, which is an ordinary two months. Parliamentary replies answer what is asked, and no reporting obligation was breached by not repeating a table nobody requested.
caseAgainst: A quantity that is compiled continuously and published intermittently is one no reader can track, and the gap is now longer than the series. The last published figure covers a period ending January 2023; three years later the Ministry's comprehensive statement of neighbourhood power cooperation gives infrastructure with no flows, and its own year-end review of 2025 does not mention Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, exports or cross-border trade in any form. Physical capacity is thereby fully described and its use is not described at all — a reader can learn how many links exist and nothing about whether power crosses them. And the one series that was published contains a comparison trap: a ten-month figure sits at the head of a column of twelve-month figures, distinguished only by a parenthesis, in a release whose headline speaks of the last four years.
differentFactsNote: The two figures for 2019-20 — 6,168.14 and 6,987.94 — are NOT a disagreement and are not filed as one. They are the same quantity measured to different cut-offs, ten months and twelve, and the difference of 819.80 Million Units is the remainder of the year. Recorded explicitly because two official figures for one financial year is the shape of a differentFacts pair, and treating it as one would manufacture a contest out of a reporting convention.

unmeasured.what: India's electricity exports to Bangladesh after January 2023
unmeasured.why: The Central Electricity Authority compiles these flows — the 2023 reply attributes the series to it — so the figures exist. They are absent from the places they would appear: the Ministry of Power's Year End Review 2025, scanned in full, contains no mention of Bangladesh, exports or cross-border trade, and the 2 April 2026 Lok Sabha reply on cooperation with neighbouring countries gives no volume over any of the thirty links it lists.

unmeasured.why: The published series ends at January 2023, which is before the period in which such an arrangement would appear in it, so the series cannot speak to the question either way. No primary establishing the arrangement was retrieved in this run or the previous one, and this record therefore asserts no absence — the point recorded is only that the measured series stops before the question becomes answerable.

caveat: The 2022-23 figure of 7,234.08 Million Units covers ten months, to January 2023, and is not comparable with the twelve-month figures above which it sits. NO ANNUALISATION IS PERFORMED HERE and none should be inferred: electricity flows are seasonal, so scaling ten months to twelve would produce a figure that describes no period and belongs to no source. For the same reason the record states no trend across the four years and no growth rate. The Year End Review 2025 counts are of a scan that saw the document — 19 occurrences of "Ministry of Power", 86 of "2025", 39 of "electricity" and 42 of "transmission" over 49,271 characters, with no `Loading` placeholder — because a zero from a page that failed to load is not an absence.

title: The debt-restructuring instrument was named in December 2024 and existed by April 2025, and the assistance around it is stated in three currencies, two of them without a rate, and never totalled
summary: At the India-Sri Lanka summit of 16 December 2024 the two leaders "instructed officials to finalize discussions on the bilateral MoU on Debt Restructuring". By the joint press statement of 5 April 2025 in Colombo the Prime Minister referred to "our bilateral 'Debt Restructuring Agreement'" as an existing instrument, and announced that in the preceding six months India had converted loans worth more than US$100 million into grants, that interest rates had been reduced that day, and that a support package of approximately 2.4 billion Lankan Rupees would be provided for the Eastern Provinces. The December statement records India as co-chair of the Official Creditors' Committee, emergency financing and forex support worth US$4 billion, and US$20.66 million to settle payments due for projects completed under existing Lines of Credit.
claimAtLaunch: Two things, and only the first is a commitment. The commitment: to finalise discussions on the bilateral MoU on Debt Restructuring, stated on 16 December 2024 with no date attached. The framing: a "strategic shift from debt-driven models towards investment led partnerships", which the two leaders agreed "would ensure a more sustainable path to economic recovery" — an assertion about a direction, carrying no target.
whatHappened: COMMITMENT STATE (a) RESOLVED, AND QUICKLY. The instrument named on 16 December 2024 as something officials were instructed to finalise is spoken of on 5 April 2025 as existing — a bilateral Debt Restructuring Agreement, referred to in the Prime Minister's own voice — which is delivery inside four months against a commitment that carried no deadline at all. THE QUANTITIES AROUND IT DO NOT COMBINE. Four figures are given across the two documents: US$4 billion of "emergency financing and forex support", US$20.66 million to settle payments due under existing Lines of Credit, "more than US$100 million" of loans converted into grants, and approximately 2.4 billion Lankan Rupees for the Eastern Provinces. They are in two currencies with no rate published, they mix a facility aggregate with specific transactions, one of them is a floor rather than a figure, and no document retrieved states a total of relief extended or debt reduced.
assessmentNote: The delivery half worked and the measurement half does not permit scoring. A named instrument moved from instruction to existence in four months, which is faster than most of this phase's commitments and is scored as such. What cannot be scored is the assistance: the figures are not commensurable, no aggregate is published, and the largest of them has no breakdown, so whether the relief was large or small against Sri Lanka's obligations is not answerable from anything retrieved. Partly, on that split — not as a hedge between the two.
caseFor: This is a commitment kept faster than it was required to be, on a matter where slowness is the norm. The December statement set no date; four months later the instrument existed and interest rates had been cut on top of it. India co-chaired the Official Creditors' Committee — a role, not a cheque, and the harder of the two things to do — and the Sri Lankan President's own account credits that co-chairing as instrumental in finalising the wider restructuring in time. Converting Lines of Credit into grants is the form of relief that actually removes debt rather than deferring it, and India did it repeatedly: US$20.66 million to clear payments due on completed projects, then more than US$100 million of loans converted over six months. The April statement also puts these figures in India's own voice, which the December one did not.
caseAgainst: Nothing here can be added up, and the presentation makes that harder rather than easier. US$4 billion covers "emergency financing and forex support" — a disbursement and a facility, which are different quantities — with no breakdown, no period and no statement of how much was drawn or repaid, so the headline figure describes neither a stock nor a flow. "More than US$100 million" is a floor and not a measurement. And the Eastern Provinces package is stated in Lankan Rupees while everything around it is in dollars, with no rate given, which leaves the smallest headline commitment in the speech carrying its largest digits — 2.4 billion beside 20.66 million. In the December statement every figure for Indian assistance sits in the Sri Lankan President's mouth, thanked for rather than asserted; the Prime Minister's own paragraph contains no number at all.
differentFactsNote: No competing accounts. The US$20.66 million of December 2024 and the "more than US$100 million" of April 2025 are not two versions of one figure and are not filed as such: the first settles payments due on completed Line of Credit projects, the second converts loans to grants over a later six-month window. Different acts, possibly overlapping, and nothing retrieved states the relationship between them — which is recorded as unmeasured rather than resolved by assumption.

unmeasured.what: The composition of the US$4 billion — how much was emergency financing, how much forex support, over what period, and how much has been drawn or repaid
unmeasured.why: The figure appears once, as a round aggregate, in the Sri Lankan President's expression of thanks. No Indian government document retrieved breaks it down, dates it, or distinguishes facility from disbursement. As with the Maldives swap in L-0206, a facility and a drawing are different quantities and the published number does not say which it is.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A Ministry of Finance or Department of Economic Affairs statement of assistance to Sri Lanka by instrument and year, or a Parliamentary answer giving the breakdown.

unmeasured.what: The total value of debt relief extended to Sri Lanka, and the exchange rate applied to the 2.4 billion Lankan Rupee package
unmeasured.why: Four figures are published across the two statements in two currencies, and no document retrieved totals them or gives a rate at which the Rupee figure could be placed beside the dollar ones. The rate exists and is not stated; the total is a sum the publishers have not performed.
unmeasured.wouldFill: An Indian government statement of cumulative assistance to Sri Lanka in one currency, or the Eastern Provinces package restated in dollars.

unmeasured.what: The text, date of signature and terms of the bilateral Debt Restructuring Agreement
unmeasured.why: It is referred to as existing on 5 April 2025 and was still being finalised on 16 December 2024, so it was concluded between those dates. Neither the date nor any term of it appears in anything retrieved, and the April reference is a sentence in a press statement rather than an announcement of the instrument.
unmeasured.wouldFill: The text of the Agreement, or a Ministry of Finance announcement of its signature and principal terms.

caveat: NO CURRENCY CONVERSION IS PERFORMED HERE. The 2.4 billion Lankan Rupee figure is not restated in dollars and is not added to any dollar figure, because no rate appears in the source and applying an external one would attach a precision to the comparison that the publisher did not offer. For the same reason no total of assistance is stated. The 5 April 2025 document is the Prime Minister's remarks at a joint press statement — a speech, not an agreement text — and this record treats its figures as announced rather than as audited. The grid interconnection is noted here only as it was framed on that occasion, as creating opportunities for Sri Lanka to export electricity; the link itself is the single India-Sri Lanka row in the Ministry of Power table recorded at L-0208, where it is also the one entry for which no operating history can exist.

title: Nineteen months after the IMEC memorandum the corridor's published scope had grown and its deliverable list was still empty, and the two figures attached to it name neither a baseline nor a date
summary: A Memorandum of Understanding on the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor was signed on 9 September 2023 at the G20 Summit in New Delhi by India, the United States, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, the European Union, Italy, France and Germany. It described an Eastern Corridor connecting India to the Gulf and a Northern Corridor connecting the Gulf to Europe, comprising a railway and ship-rail transit network and road transport routes. An Inter-Governmental Framework Agreement with the United Arab Emirates was signed on 13 February 2024 and given ex-post facto Cabinet approval on 13 March 2024. On 16 April 2025 the Minister of Commerce and Industry told a High-Level Roundtable that IMEC would "bring down logistics costs by up to 30%, reduce transportation time by 40%", and set out five suggestions for how the initiative should be taken forward.
claimAtLaunch: At signature, a description rather than a target: two corridors, a set of transport modes, and economic integration between India and Europe. The only quantified claims appear nineteen months later and are benefit claims, not commitments — costs down by up to 30 per cent and transport time down by 40 per cent. No completion date, no phasing, no cost, no route length and no segment target appears in any document retrieved.
whatHappened: THE SCOPE GREW WHILE THE DELIVERABLE LIST STAYED EMPTY. The 2023 memorandum described a railway and ship-rail network and road routes. By April 2025 the published account added energy pipelines, clean energy infrastructure and undersea cables, and raised the possibility of extending connectivity to Africa through the Middle East. Across the same nineteen months no kilometre built, no contract awarded, no cost, no financing arrangement and no completed segment appears in anything retrieved. WHAT THE MINISTER SET OUT WAS FIVE SUGGESTIONS, NOT FIVE DELIVERABLES: that the corridor be viewed through a public-private partnership lens because leaving it to government "would limit its efficiency and financial viability"; that regulatory connectivity be pursued; that financing instruments including "IMEC Bonds" be created; that industry bodies be engaged; and that think tanks and academia be brought into "the visioning and design process". Nineteen months after signature, the design was still being visioned and the money was still to be raised.
assessmentNote: Commitment state (d) — unfalsifiable by construction, and the second instance the instrument holds after L-0209. No completion date, no phasing and no target quantity means there is no trigger, so it is not state (a); it can never fall due, so it cannot reach (b); and nothing evidences abandonment, so it is not (c). Scored no-objective on that ground: an objective is a target that can be failed. This is NOT a finding that IMEC is stalled or abandoned — it is that nothing published permits either conclusion, now or at any future date.
caseFor: Eight parties including the United States, the European Union and Saudi Arabia put their names to a single connectivity instrument, which is itself the hard part and is not nothing. India converted the multilateral memorandum into a bilateral treaty instrument with the United Arab Emirates within five months and took it to Cabinet, which is faster than most of the agreements in this phase moved and is the concrete step available to a party that cannot build the other legs alone. The five suggestions are also more candid than announcements of this kind usually are: they name the real obstacles rather than asserting them solved — that government financing alone will not carry it, that regulatory and customs harmonisation matters as much as track, that new instruments will be needed to fund it. A transcontinental corridor across sovereign jurisdictions genuinely takes longer than nineteen months, and declining to name a date may be honesty about that rather than evasion.
caseAgainst: The two figures that circulate are the two that cannot be checked. "Up to 30%" is a ceiling rather than an estimate, and neither figure names a baseline route, a current cost, a comparator corridor, a cargo type or a source; a reader is given the size of a saving without being told what it is a saving against. Meanwhile the corridor's described components multiplied — pipelines, clean energy infrastructure, undersea cables, a possible extension to Africa — while nothing retrieved records a metre of it being built, and an initiative whose scope grows faster than its output is the shape that most reliably outruns scrutiny. The Ministry that signed the bilateral framework recorded IMEC in its own year-end account of 2024 solely as the signing of that agreement. And a minister proposing, nineteen months in, that the private sector lead and that bonds be invented to fund the thing is describing an initiative whose financing was not settled when it was announced.

unmeasured.what: The baseline against which logistics costs fall by up to 30 per cent and transport time by 40 per cent
unmeasured.why: Both are share-shaped figures with neither term named. No comparator route, current cost, cargo type, measurement method or source is given in the release or in anything else retrieved, so neither figure can be checked, and the direction of any error cannot even be bounded.
unmeasured.wouldFill: The study or model the figures are drawn from, or a Ministry of Commerce statement of the comparator route and cost base.

unmeasured.what: Any physical or financial progress on the corridor — kilometres, contracts, cost, or a completed segment
unmeasured.why: The Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways signed the bilateral framework and would build the maritime leg; its Year End Review 2024 mentions IMEC three times and all three are the signature of that agreement, with no progress attached. The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade's Year End Review 2025 does not mention IMEC at all. Its twelve occurrences of "corridor" are the National Industrial Corridor Development Programme, a domestic scheme, which is why the word count is not treated as evidence either way.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways or Ministry of Commerce statement of IMEC works undertaken, or a Parliamentary answer on expenditure and physical progress.

unmeasured.what: A completion date, phasing schedule or interim milestone of any kind
unmeasured.why: None appears in the memorandum, the Inter-Governmental Framework Agreement announcement, or the April 2025 remarks. A date that was never set does not exist to be published, which is what separates this from the two items above.
unmeasured.wouldFill: Any published schedule for either corridor, or a target year stated by any signatory.

caveat: The most recent Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways year-end account retrieved is for 2024; a 2025 edition was not located, so the Ports-side position after December 2024 is UNCHECKED rather than established as empty, and this record does not claim otherwise. The nineteen-month and thirty-five-month intervals are elapsed periods between published dates and are not claims about how long any work took. The April 2025 document is a minister's remarks at a roundtable — a speech, not an agreement or a progress report — and its figures are recorded as announced, not as audited. This record makes no assertion about conditions in the regions the corridor would cross, because nothing bearing on them was retrieved.

title: India joined the WTO fisheries agreement as the 123rd member to do so, ten months after it took effect without India, and the release naming three specific negotiating asks in 2024 has no successor saying whether any was obtained
summary: India deposited its Instrument of Acceptance of the WTO Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies on 20 July 2026, becoming the 123rd Member to do so. The Agreement was adopted by consensus at the 12th Ministerial Conference in Geneva in June 2022 and entered into force on 15 September 2025 after acceptance by two-thirds of Members. It covers subsidies to marine wild capture fishing and fishing-related activities at sea; aquaculture and inland fisheries are outside its scope. In its Year End Review of December 2024 the Department of Commerce had stated three specific asks in the fisheries subsidies negotiations: longer transition periods, a permanent carve-out for small-scale and artisanal fishers without geographical limitations, and a carve-out of Exclusive Economic Zones.
claimAtLaunch: The Department of Commerce, December 2024: "India is actively engaging in the ongoing fisheries subsidies negotiations to protect the interests of its fisheries communities. India has requested for longer transition periods, permanent carve out for small scale and artisanal fishers without geographical limitations, and a carve out of EEZs to protect the sovereign rights of developing countries." India also raised concerns about the proposed dilution of disciplines for distant water fishing nations.
whatHappened: THE ACT IS DATED AND RANKED, AND THAT IS RARE IN THIS ARC. India acceded four years and one month after the Agreement was adopted, and ten months after it entered into force without India, as the 123rd depositing Member — the WTO's deposit sequence makes the timing measurable in a way almost nothing else here is. WHAT THE ACCESSION SECURED IS NOT STATED. The acceptance release does not mention transition periods, the artisanal carve-out or the EEZ carve-out, and does not say whether those asks were met, dropped, or belong to the continuing negotiation rather than to this instrument. It asserts benefits without quantifying any: no number of fishers protected, no value of subsidies disciplined, no share of India's catch affected, no estimate of the gain from constraining distant-water fleets.
assessmentNote: The accession is complete, dated and verifiable, and the release names real domestic implementing instruments rather than gesturing at them. What cannot be scored is the objective the Department stated in 2024 — protecting the interests of fisheries communities through three named asks — because nothing published says whether any was obtained. A caution belongs in the score itself: the December 2024 asks describe "ongoing" negotiations, and it is not stated whether they attach to this Agreement or to the unconcluded further negotiation on overcapacity and overfishing. This record therefore does NOT treat acceptance as abandonment of the asks; it records that the two statements cannot be joined from what either says.
caseFor: Joining is the substantive act and India did it with the domestic machinery already in place, which is the harder half. The release names specific instruments rather than intentions — the Sustainable Harnessing of Fisheries in the Exclusive Economic Zone Rules 2025 and the Guidelines for Sustainable Harnessing of Fisheries in the High Seas by Indian-Flagged Fishing Vessels 2025 — so implementation capacity is asserted against named regulations. The Agreement's disciplines fall hardest on large subsidised industrial fleets operated by distant water fishing nations, which is the category India is not in and had objected to seeing diluted, so the instrument runs with India's stated interest rather than against it. And the release is candid about the limit of its own reach: it says plainly that aquaculture and inland fisheries are outside scope and that aquaculture-based shrimp predominates in India's seafood exports, which is a concession that the Agreement's bite on India's export sector is small.
caseAgainst: Four years and one month from adoption to acceptance, and ten months after the Agreement was already binding on others, is a delay the government's own release makes measurable and does not explain. Being the 123rd Member to deposit is a position in a sequence India published itself, and no reason for it appears anywhere retrieved. More consequentially, the three asks stated in December 2024 simply vanish from the record: a government that publicly names what it is negotiating for owes a reader some statement of what it got, and the acceptance release supplies none — a reader cannot tell whether the carve-outs were won, conceded, or deferred to a negotiation that has not concluded. Every benefit claimed is qualitative, so even the direction of the effect on Indian fishers is unquantified.

unmeasured.what: Whether India obtained longer transition periods, the permanent carve-out for small-scale and artisanal fishers, or the EEZ carve-out
unmeasured.why: The three asks were stated by the Department of Commerce in December 2024. The acceptance release of 20 July 2026 does not mention any of them, and no document retrieved records their outcome. It is also not stated whether they attach to this Agreement or to the continuing negotiation, so the question cannot even be posed precisely from published material.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A Department of Commerce statement of the negotiating outcome against its stated asks, or a Parliamentary answer on what the Agreement's flexibilities give India.

unmeasured.what: The reason for the four-year interval between adoption and acceptance
unmeasured.why: The release gives both dates and no account of the gap. Whether it reflects negotiation, domestic legal process, or a decision to await entry into force is not stated anywhere retrieved.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A Ministry statement or Parliamentary answer on the timing of ratification.

unmeasured.what: The quantitative effect on Indian fishers — subsidies disciplined, fishers covered, or catch affected
unmeasured.why: Every benefit in the release is asserted qualitatively. No baseline of Indian fisheries subsidies, no count of affected vessels or fishers, and no share of catch appears, so the Agreement's magnitude for India is not established in either direction.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A Department of Fisheries or Commerce assessment of the Agreement's application to Indian subsidy programmes.

caveat: NO RATIO IS COMPUTED FROM 123. The Department of Commerce gives WTO membership as 166 following the accession of Comoros and Timor-Leste at the 13th Ministerial Conference in March 2024; the 123rd-depositor figure is from July 2026. Those are two different documents at two different dates and membership is not asserted to be unchanged between them, so a share of members would be a derived quantity resting on an assumption neither source makes. The two elapsed intervals — four years and one month from adoption, ten months from entry into force — are periods between published dates and carry no claim about what occurred within them. On public stockholding, the Department's December 2024 statement records only that there was no outcome on agriculture at the 13th Ministerial Conference and that India opposed attempts to divert focus from the Permanent Solution; no record is made here of that arc, which remains open.

title: Vaccine Maitri is presented as a gift, and the doses the government names as gifted are 1.51 crore of a stated 30.12 crore supplied
summary: A Press Information Bureau explainer of 18 June 2025 states that since January 2021 India supplied over 30.12 crore vaccine doses to 99 countries and two United Nations bodies under the Vaccine Maitri initiative, and that this "included 1.51 crore doses gifted to over 50 nations and 5.2 crore doses through the COVAX mechanism". The two named channels together account for 6.71 crore doses, leaving at least 23.41 crore — a little over three-quarters of the stated total — in neither category. The same explainer describes the initiative as "a testament to its human-centric diplomacy" under the heading "Humanity First, Always".
claimAtLaunch: No target, quantity or date is announced anywhere in the document. What is offered is a characterisation: humanity first, human-centric diplomacy, and India as "a reliable partner for global health and a compassionate voice from the Global South". The numbers are given as achievement, not as progress against anything.
whatHappened: THE TOTAL IS A SUPPLY FIGURE AND THE FRAMING IS A GIFT FRAMING, AND ONLY ONE OF THE THREE NUMBERS IS ABOUT GIVING. Of the 30.12 crore doses stated as supplied, 1.51 crore are described as gifted — just over five per cent, on the government's own two figures — and 5.2 crore went through COVAX, a multilateral procurement and allocation mechanism rather than a bilateral gift. The remaining 23.41 crore doses at minimum are placed in no category at all. NOTHING RETRIEVED SAYS WHAT THEY WERE. The word "included" is accurate and does not claim to exhaust the total, which is why this is recorded as a composition that cannot be reconstructed rather than as a false statement.
assessmentNote: The initiative announces no target, no quantity and no date, so there is nothing against which it could have worked or failed, and the numbers are presented as accomplishment rather than as progress. What can be checked is the composition of what is reported, and the finding is that it cannot be reconstructed from the figures given. Recorded so that the 30.12 crore is not later read as a measure of doses given away, which is the reading the surrounding language invites and the figures do not support.
caseFor: The disclosure is more specific than the framing required and that cuts in the government's favour. It would have been easy to publish only the 30.12 crore total under a humanitarian heading; instead the explainer breaks out the gifted doses and the COVAX doses separately, with the gifted figure to two decimal places, which is what makes the composition question askable at all. "Included" is the correct word for a partial breakdown and does not assert that the two named channels exhaust the total. Supplying 30.12 crore doses to 99 countries and two UN bodies from a standing start in January 2021 is a real logistical achievement whatever the commercial mix, and reaching two UN bodies and over 50 nations by gift is not a trivial share of the world. COVAX doses are also not self-interested in any ordinary sense: they went to a multilateral allocation mechanism that decided their destination.
caseAgainst: The number that travels is 30.12 crore and the frame it travels under is a gift, and those two things do not describe the same thing. On the government's own figures the explicitly gifted portion is 1.51 crore of 30.12 crore — a little over one dose in twenty — while the heading above them reads "Humanity First, Always". More than three-quarters of the stated total is assigned to no channel whatever, so a reader cannot tell what the largest part of the programme actually was, and no other retrieved document supplies it. Four years after the period began, an explainer written to summarise India's global footprint gives a composition that cannot be reconstructed, which is a choice about presentation rather than a limit of the underlying records.

unmeasured.what: What the 23.41 crore doses outside the gifted and COVAX categories were — the channel, terms and recipients
unmeasured.why: The explainer names two channels and a larger total and does not describe the difference. Nothing retrieved states what the remainder consisted of. This record does NOT name a candidate: the obvious inference is not supported by any document retrieved, and an unsourced explanation would be as much of a fabrication as an unsourced accusation.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A Ministry of External Affairs or Ministry of Health statement of Vaccine Maitri supplies by channel, or a Parliamentary answer breaking the total into grant, commercial and multilateral components.

unmeasured.what: The value of the doses supplied, on any basis
unmeasured.why: The programme is reported in doses only. No cost, price or value appears in the explainer or in anything else retrieved, so the scale of what was given, sold or contributed cannot be stated in money at all.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A budgetary figure for Vaccine Maitri, or a Parliamentary answer on expenditure and receipts under the initiative.

caveat: The stated total is "over 30.12 crore", a floor rather than an exact figure, so the residual of 23.41 crore is a MINIMUM and is stated as such — a larger true total makes the unassigned share larger, not smaller, and this record does not compute a share of a floor as though it were exact. The two share figures given — just over five per cent gifted, about twenty-two per cent across both named channels — take 30.12 crore as the denominator and the government's own 1.51 and 5.2 crore as numerators, and are stated with both terms named for that reason. "Over 50 nations" qualifies the number of countries, not the 1.51 crore doses. The explainer is a Press Information Bureau summary written in June 2025 about a period beginning January 2021; it is treated as the government's own restatement, not as the underlying record of supplies.
